title: Money and Banking
1  Banks and Financial Intermediation
text:
1.1 Banks and their Financial Statements
The vast majority of economic transactions today use money kept in bank deposits to pay for goods and services.
Banks play a key role in the financial system and in the economy and much of the influence that central banks have on the economy via monetary policy works through the influence that it has on the banking system.
The banking sector also played a key role in many major historical crises, including the Great Depression, the global recession of 2008-09, Ireland’s economic crisis of 2008-11 and the “euro crisis” of 2010-12. And sometimes, you see large banks getting in trouble in “normal” times, like when Credit Suisse and Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) failed in 2023.
In these notes, we will start with a simple introduction to banks and their role in the economy. As the course goes on, we will introduce more complex topics, focusing on banking crises and their impacts as well as issues related to banking regulation.

title: 1  Banks and Financial Intermediation
text:
1.1.1 The Origin of Banking
Though it is a fascinating topic, we will not have time to cover the history of coins and paper money being accepted as means of payment. However, once money became widely accepted as a way to conduct transactions, the question arose of where people stored their money.
You could keep it all at home (perhaps under the mattress) but this would not be very safe.
Banks began as safe depositories for cash: You had your own separate locker in the bank’s vaults for your cash. And you could go to the bank when you needed to get out your cash. Of course, the bank would charge you some fees to secure your money.
But why waste your time going yourself? Why not pay your bills with a special piece of paper (clearly identifiable as coming from you) that says the bearer is entitled to payment of cash from your account? In other words, you can write a cheque.
Once many people had bank accounts, then they weren’t taking money out of the bank after receiving a cheque. Instead, they were instructing the bank to move cash from someone else’s locker to theirs. This means banking not only secure your money, but also take the responsibility of payments.


1.1.2 History of Central Banks
Suppose Bank A’s depositors ask to have their accounts credited by \(€10\) million by presenting cheques from Bank B’s depositors. At the same time, Bank B’s depositors ask to be credited \(€15\) million from Bank A depositors. How do we settle these demands?
We could send \(€19\) million in cash around town to the various vaults. But the couriers could get held up by bandits!
A better idea was the following: Settle accounts at a “clearing house” bank. At end of the day, the clearing house orders the transfer of \(€1\) million from B’s vaults to A’s. Actually, the clearing house could mingle all the cash together and just deduct \(€1\) million from the ledger entry for Bank B’s account and add it to Bank A’s.
These clearing houses were the forerunners of today’s central banks. Today, all commercial banks in a country maintain an account with their country’s central bank.
Note again that lots of transactions are happening without any cash being withdrawn.
At this stage, all deposits were still backed by cash; banks had not yet fully begun to “create credit.”


1.1.3 Fractional-Reserve Banking
Most of the time (and most here is a very important qualifier!) only a small fraction of a bank’s total deposits will be withdrawn on any given day. And new money also gets deposited every day. Consider the example on the previous section: Despite \(€10\) million in total claims against it, Bank B still only needed to hand over \(€1\)million at the end of the day.
At some point, there was a “eureka moment”: Why do we have to keep all this cash sitting around doing nothing to back up the deposits? Why not loan out some of these deposits and just keep enough cash reserves on hand to deal with day-to-day demands?
And so, fractional-reserve banking was born: Banks don’t keep all your money in a vault anymore. They lend it out to other people. This is called fractional-reserve banking because banks only keep a fraction of the money people have deposited with them “on reserve” in case people come looking for their money.

1.1.4 Net Interest Margins and Bank Profits
Banks earn profits mainly from the gap between interest received on assets and interest paid on liabilities. This difference is the net interest; expressed as a rate gap it is the net interest margin.
Overnight deposits—funds available to withdraw anytime—pay lower rates than time deposits (where you agree to wait one year or more to take your money out.) The low rate on overnight deposits reflects a convenience yield: People accept low interest rates on these deposits to get immediate access and payment ability.

1.1.6 Advantages of Fractional Reserve Banking
Fractional-reserve banking has generated a lot of criticism over the years along the lines of “how dare these people pretend they have your money when they’ve actually given it to someone else.”
Don’t take these criticisms too seriously. Banks don’t pretend they have your money in the vault but they will (almost always) give you your money back on request if you ask.
But fractional-reserve banking has important advantages:

Saves Depositors Money: Banks can charge interest on their loans. Without this interest income, the only way a bank can make a profit is to charge fees to depositors. Interest earned can be used as an alternative source of income for banks and (assuming competition between banks) this reduces the need for fees related to safeguarding their money.
Financial Intermediation: It makes banks an intermediary between those that have money and those that need to borrow money. They take money from some people and lend it out to others. This financial intermediation function is a crucial element of the modern economy.

Why can’t those with savings just lend them directly to those who want to borrow? i.e why not just have peer-to-peer lending?

Pooling Savings: Many savers deposit small amounts. Someone looking for a big loan can get it from a bank rather than having to look for a saver with the correct amount of funds.
Risk Diversification: Savers lending their funds to an individual borrower face idiosyncratic risk. If that borrower fails to pay back, they lose everything. The bank can lend to many borrowers, take its cut, and pass a safe return back to the saver.
Information Processing: Banks can specialize in screening borrowers, processing and sharing information, and in writing sophisticated debt contracts.
Maturity Transformation: If I want to have my savings back when I want them, I won’t lend the money for one year or more, as borrowers may want.

Therefore, the essence of financial intermediation is to pool dispersed funds and reallocate them across different individuals, time periods, and risk profiles. Banks can make these long-term loans, knowing that (hopefully) each period, only some of its depositors will want their money back.

1.2 Some Bogus Debunking
There is a popular argument stating: “Banks are not financial intermediaries; since loans create deposits, banks do not need to hold deposits before they can issue loans.” While this view seizes upon a specific accounting detail, it exaggerates it into an erroneous conclusion. We illustrate the accounting process of “loans creating deposits” to explain why this argument is incorrect.
Suppose our bank makes a loan for €10 to Lucy. In some cases, the bank opens a special deposit account with their own bank and tells Lucy she can get her €10 from it.

In other words, the bank’s loan assets increase by €10 because Lucy owes the bank €10. At the same time, the bank’s deposit liabilities also increase by €10 because Lucy now has an additional €10 in her account.
This is what “loans create deposits” means. It does not mean that the bank has created additional resources out of thin air that it can freely use. Rather, it means that at the moment a loan is issued, the bank can record the transaction by simultaneously expanding both sides of its balance sheet.
Indeed, it appears that the bank has created a loan and a deposit without first raising funds from anyone else. From this perspective, it may seem that banks are not financial intermediaries.
However, the question is: Why does Lucy borrow money in the first place? She certainly does not borrow €10 just to leave it sitting in her bank account, especially since the interest rate she pays on the loan is typically higher than the interest she earns on her deposits. Instead, she borrows money to finance consumption or investment.
Suppose Lucy uses the loan to buy a car. She purchases the car from Evil Elmo, a car dealership whose bank account is held at another bank, X Bank. To complete the payment, Lucy needs her bank to transfer the money to X Bank, which then credits the dealership’s account.
This means that Lucy’s bank must transfer funds to X Bank. Typically, this interbank payment is settled through reserve accounts held at the central bank: the reserve balance of Lucy’s bank decreases, while the reserve balance of X Bank increases.
As a result, the balance sheet of Lucy’s bank becomes:

Two things have happened here:
First, the loan still exists, so the bank’s loan assets remain at €105.
Second, Lucy’s €10 deposit has been transferred out of her bank, so the bank’s total deposits return to €100. At the same time, to settle the payment to X Bank, the bank’s cash and reserves decrease from €15 to €5.
When a bank issues a loan, it can create a corresponding deposit. However, once the borrower spends the money and the payment is transferred to another bank, the lending bank must use its reserves to settle the transaction.
Therefore, banks cannot simply “create loans out of thin air” without limits. They are still constrained by their funding sources, reserve availability, liquidity requirements, and regulatory restrictions.
Thus, the statement “loans create deposits” is perfectly valid from an accounting perspective. However, it does not imply that banks do not need funding or that banks are not financial intermediaries.

1.2.1 Further Debunking

Not How Large Loans Work: The “give Lucy a deposit account” story is correct for small personal loans but it’s not how most loans work. With mortgage loans, the money is usually sent to a lawyer who then ensures the seller obtains the funds and that the buyer obtains the legal deeds for the property. Car loan funds are commonly issued directly to dealerships selling the cars with the bank obtaining a title deed for the car.
Bond Borrowing: If banks can expand their lending without having to source funds, why do they bother borrowing money in the form of interest-bearing bonds to obtain funding for their activities?
Borrowing from Money Markets or the Central Bank?

The debunkers have a response to the idea that banks need to have reserves to make loans: No, they can just borrow from other banks or from central banks. As much as they want! Banks can make as many loans as they want.
This is utter nonsense, contradicting both basic banking regulations, the role central banks play when loaning money to banks and many of the lessons from the global financial crisis.

title: 1  Banks and Financial Intermediation
text:
1.3 Instability
Having listed all the advantages of fractional-reserve banking, it turns out there is also a very important disadvantage associated with it. Banks are supposed to have assets greater than liabilities owed to non-investors (i.e. positive bank capital). What if the bank makes bad loans to borrowers that default? What if customers suspect the bank does not have assets to pay back money to depositors?
If this happens, the earlier arguments that only some customers wanting their money back may turn out to be incorrect. We may have a run on the bank: Lots of depositors look to get their money back. Banks usually find it difficult to cope with these runs.
For these reasons, fractional reserve banking systems are subject to occasional periods of instability.
We mentioned “maturity transformation” as one of the cool features of fractional reserve banking. But when things are going badly for banks, you are more likely to hear about maturity mismatch i.e. the fact that the average maturity of a bank’s assets is longer than the average maturity of its liabilities.
Most banks are thus vulnerable if situations arise in which there are demands to pay back a large amount of liabilities over a short period of time. They have loaned out large amounts of money in the form of, for example, 30-year mortgages and they are not able to call these people up and say “We’re in a spot of bother. We know we said you could pay back over 30 years but could you instead pay it all back now?”
Banks also have legally binding contracts with depositors, e.g. people with “’demand deposits” have been told they can get their money out on demand. These two sets of legal contracts cannot always be jointly honoured.
In the past, governments imposed regulations to limit maturity mismatch: Mortgage lenders took in longer-term savings, banks that had demand deposits only made shorter loans. However, these restrictions have generally been lifted over the years.

title: 2  Liquidity and Solvency
text:
2.1 Examples
This section introduces two fundamental concepts in banking: liquidity and solvency. Although both are essential to a bank’s financial health, they refer to different aspects of its balance sheet. Consider the following simplified example.
The following accounting identity always holds:
\[
\text{Equity Capital}=\text{Assets}-\text{Liabilities}
\]
Thus, equity capital is the difference between the value of a bank’s assets and the value of its liabilities. Conceptually, it is the residual value that would belong to shareholders if the bank could sell all its assets at their stated values and use the proceeds to repay all its liabilities.
Four points are especially important:
Liquidity and solvency are conceptually distinct, but they can interact—and reinforce each other—during a banking crisis.

The central distinction is:

Solvency: Are the bank’s total assets worth enough to cover its liabilities?
Liquidity: Can the bank obtain the cash needed to meet its short-term payment obligations when they come due?

title: 2  Liquidity and Solvency
section: 2.2 The Relationship Between Liquidity and Solvency
text:
2.2 The Relationship Between Liquidity and Solvency

2.2.1 1. Doubts About Solvency Can Trigger a Liquidity Crisis
If depositors believe that a bank may be insolvent, they may fear that it will eventually be unable to repay everyone. To avoid potential losses, they may rush to withdraw their deposits, creating a bank run.
Large, simultaneous withdrawals can rapidly exhaust the bank’s cash and other liquid assets. Normally, a bank facing a temporary shortage of cash might borrow in financial markets. But if other banks and investors also doubt its financial condition, they may refuse to lend. The bank can then face a severe liquidity crisis.
The key mechanism is that concerns about solvency can create an immediate liquidity problem—even before insolvency has been conclusively established.


2.2.2 2. A Liquidity Crisis Can Lead to Insolvency
A bank facing heavy withdrawals may be forced to sell assets quickly to raise cash. Under distressed market conditions, those assets may have to be sold at a substantial discount.
For example, suppose an asset with a book value of €100 can be sold for only €70. The sale generates a €30 loss, reducing the bank’s equity capital. If such losses are sufficiently large, an initially solvent bank may become insolvent.
This illustrates how a liquidity problem can turn into a solvency problem. Although liquidity and solvency are different concepts, banking crises can produce a self-reinforcing interaction between them.

title: 2  Liquidity and Solvency
section: 2.3 Measuring Solvency: Why Equity Capital Can Be Difficult to Assess
text:
2.3 Measuring Solvency: Why Equity Capital Can Be Difficult to Assess
The definition of equity capital is straightforward, but measuring it accurately can be difficult because the value of a bank’s assets is often uncertain. In particular:

Banks may overstate asset values. A troubled bank has an incentive to report optimistic asset valuations, making its equity capital appear larger than it really is.
External auditors may fail to prevent overvaluation. Auditors are expected to assess the reliability of financial statements, but their judgments may be affected by incentives, including a desire to retain clients.
Reported book equity may therefore be misleading. A bank may publish accounts showing positive equity capital even when the economic value of its assets is insufficient to cover its liabilities. Depositors, investors, and regulators may consequently treat reported capital figures with skepticism.

In short, assessing solvency depends critically on asset valuation. Information asymmetries and possible misreporting make the true financial position of a troubled bank difficult for outsiders to determine.
In principle, a central bank acting as the lender of last resort can provide emergency liquidity assistance to a bank that is solvent but temporarily illiquid. The central challenge, however, is determining whether the bank is genuinely solvent. Providing liquidity to a bank that is already insolvent may merely postpone the resolution of its losses and potentially shift costs to the public sector.
Example: The Irish banking crisis of 2008. On September 29, 2008, Irish banks sought government liquidity support, arguing that they were fundamentally sound and faced only temporary funding difficulties. The Irish government responded by guaranteeing almost all of their liabilities. The banks were subsequently found not to be fundamentally solvent, and honoring the guarantee imposed enormous costs. The episode illustrates the dangers of mistaking a solvency problem for a temporary liquidity shortage.

2.4 Book Value and Market Value of Equity

2.4.1 1. Book Value of Equity
The book value of equity is the difference between the values of assets and liabilities reported in a bank’s accounting statements:
\[
\text{Book Equity}=\text{Book Value of Assets}-\text{Book Value of Liabilities}
\]
It is important not to interpret equity capital as cash that has been set aside. When regulators require a bank to increase its capital, they are not asking it to keep an additional pile of idle cash. Rather, a higher equity share means that shareholders absorb a larger share of potential asset losses before creditors are affected.

For example, it could issue 50 in new equity and use the proceeds to repay 50 in debt, leaving the asset side unchanged after both transactions.
The higher equity ratio does not mean that 50 in cash has been locked away and made unavailable for lending. In practice, higher capital requirements may affect banks’ funding costs, shareholders’ required returns, and lending decisions. But these effects arise through financing and risk-bearing incentives, not because equity capital is a segregated cash reserve.
Note: This example uses a simple equity-to-total-assets ratio for illustration; it is not intended to represent every feature of regulatory capital adequacy ratios.


2.4.2 2. Market Value of Equity
The market value of equity is the total stock-market value of a bank’s shares—that is, the amount investors would have to pay, at prevailing share prices, to purchase all of its outstanding equity.
Unlike book equity, market equity reflects investors’ expectations about future developments, including the bank’s profitability, dividend payments, asset quality, and risks. Historically, the market value of bank equity was often higher than its book value because investors expected banks to generate future profits.
However, many major banks have traded at market-to-book ratios below one, particularly in the period following the global financial crisis. The lecture illustrates this with a Financial Times comparison of major global banks as of November 2022.






Figure 2.1: market-to-book ratios of major global banks as of November 2022.



A market-to-book ratio below one can suggest that investors doubt whether reported asset values and expected future earnings fully justify the bank’s book equity. It does not, by itself, establish that the bank is insolvent.
Market valuations therefore provide a useful, though imperfect, signal when evaluating the credibility of a bank’s reported equity capital.

title: 2  Liquidity and Solvency
text:
2.5 Banking Regulation
Because banks can encounter both liquidity shortages and solvency problems, governments and banking regulators impose different types of prudential requirements.

2.5.1 1. Liquidity Regulations
The objective of liquidity regulation is to ensure that banks can meet withdrawals and other short-term payment obligations, including during periods of financial stress.

Reserve requirements. Banks may be required to maintain a minimum fraction of deposits in cash or balances held at the central bank.
Restrictions on maturity mismatch. Historically, some regulations limited the extent to which financial institutions could finance long-term lending with short-term deposits. For example, mortgage lenders could be required to attract longer-term deposits, while banks funded by demand deposits were restricted to shorter-term loans. Many such restrictions were later removed.
Requirements for liquid assets. More recent regulatory approaches seek to ensure that banks hold sufficient liquid assets to withstand substantial withdrawals or funding disruptions.



2.5.2 2. Solvency Regulations (Capital Adequacy Requirements)
Solvency regulation, also called capital adequacy regulation, determines the amount of equity capital banks are required to maintain relative to their activities. In general, larger banks and banks with greater risk exposures are expected to maintain more capital to absorb potential losses.
The essential distinction is summarized below:








Type of Regulation
Main Focus
Primary Objective




Liquidity regulation
Cash, central bank reserves, and other liquid assets
Ensure that banks can meet short-term payment obligations.


Solvency regulation
Equity capital and the bank’s capacity to absorb losses
Reduce the likelihood that losses will leave the bank’s assets worth less than its liabilities.



Final takeaway: Liquidity concerns a bank’s ability to pay on time, whereas solvency concerns whether the value of its assets exceeds its liabilities. A bank can be liquid but insolvent, or solvent but illiquid. Effective banking supervision must therefore address both dimensions.

text:
3.2 Money Creation
Historically, governments could issue coins or paper money and use the revenue from issuing currency to finance public expenditure. In modern advanced economies, however, the creation of central bank money is primarily carried out by central banks rather than directly by fiscal authorities.
The discussion in this section concerns money created by central banks, rather than the deposit money created when commercial banks extend loans. Here, money primarily refers to central bank money, also called base money.
Central bank money consists of:

Currency in circulation: Banknotes and coins held by the public.
Bank reserves: Balances held by commercial banks in accounts at the central bank.

The process by which commercial banks create deposit money is a separate topic.

3.2.1 Open Market Operations
The famous Nobel prize winning economist, Milton Friedman, used a “helicopter drop” of cash as a simple analogy for central bank money creation. Since helicopter drops are not practical or fair, in practice, central banks create money via methods such as open market operations:
Open market operations (OMOs) involve central bank purchases or sales of securities, such as government bonds. Consider the example from the lecture:

The central bank purchases a bond worth $1,000 from Janet.
In exchange, the central bank gives Janet a cheque for $1,000.
Janet deposits the cheque at her commercial bank, OmoBank.
OmoBank presents the cheque to the central bank for payment.
The central bank credits OmoBank’s reserve account by $1,000.

This raises a fundamental question:

Where does the central bank obtain the $1,000 that it credits to OmoBank’s reserve account?

It does not need to obtain the money from elsewhere. The central bank creates the additional reserves by crediting OmoBank’s account.
This is one mechanism through which a central bank creates base money. Importantly, the money initially created in this example takes the form of reserve balances, not newly printed banknotes. Janet also receives a new bank deposit, which is a liability of OmoBank rather than of the central bank.
If bank customers subsequently withdraw cash from ATMs, OmoBank can obtain banknotes from the central bank. Its reserve account is debited by the corresponding amount. In this way, bank reserves are exchanged for physical currency; the exchange itself does not create additional base money.







Form of central bank money
Explanation




Bank reserves
Electronic balances held by commercial banks at the central bank


Currency
Physical notes and coins supplied through the banking system and held by the public



We can understand this operation more precisely by examining how it affects the balance sheets of Janet, OmoBank, and the central bank.

3.2.1.1 Is Janet Wealthier?
No, not as a direct result of the transaction. Janet initially owns a bond worth $1,000. After selling it to the central bank, she holds a bank deposit worth $1,000 instead.



Before the transaction
After the transaction




Bond: $1,000
Bank deposit: $1,000



Janet’s portfolio composition changes, but the transaction does not immediately change her total wealth: she has exchanged one asset for another of equal value.


3.2.1.2 Is OmoBank Wealthier?
No. OmoBank receives an additional $1,000 in reserves, but it simultaneously incurs an additional $1,000 deposit liability to Janet.

Since OmoBank’s assets and liabilities increase by the same amount, its equity capital (net worth) remains unchanged.

The central bank acquires a bond worth $1,000 and creates a corresponding $1,000 reserve liability to OmoBank.

The central bank’s assets and liabilities both increase by $1,000, so its accounting capital does not change at the time of the transaction.



3.2.2 Loans to Commercial Banks
Purchasing securities is not the only way a central bank can create money. It can also lend directly to commercial banks.
For example, the Eurosystem—the European Central Bank (ECB) and the national central banks of euro-area countries—provides loans to commercial banks at specified interest rates. Traditionally, the rate on these lending operations was a key ECB policy rate.
To obtain such a loan, a commercial bank must generally pledge eligible assets as collateral. The purpose of collateral is to protect the central bank against the borrower’s failure to repay:

If a commercial bank fails to repay its loan, the central bank may claim the pledged collateral to recover the amount owed.

As with an open market purchase, the central bank supplies the loan by crediting the commercial bank’s reserve account, thereby creating additional reserves.

Change in central bank liabilities

The central bank obtains a loan asset and simultaneously creates a reserve liability. The commercial bank acquires additional reserves and incurs a corresponding borrowing liability.

However, central bank liabilities differ fundamentally from the liabilities of ordinary commercial banks or nonfinancial firms. For example, the cash that is in circulation is not in any meaningful sense a liability of the central bank. The central bank does not pay interest on cash notes and does not make any promise to swap the notes for some quantity of gold or some other asset.
Reserve balances are somewhat different. They are liabilities of the central bank, and major central banks now generally pay interest on them. Nevertheless, reserve liabilities differ from ordinary debt in several ways:

A central bank can create additional reserves rather than first borrowing money from another institution.
Reserve balances do not have a contractual maturity date on which the central bank must repay a fixed principal amount.
The central bank determines the interest rate paid on reserves as part of its monetary policy framework.
Reserve interest rates can even be negative, as they were in the Eurosystem for several years.

3.3.2 Income Statements
Due to their money creating activities, central banks build up large stocks of assets over time. The central bank may subsequently earn a profit if the interest income on the bond exceeds the interest it pays on the newly created reserves, after allowing for relevant expenses. More generally, a central bank’s income may come from several sources:

Interest earned on securities, including government bonds.
Interest earned on loans to commercial banks.
The ability to issue currency, which generally pays no interest to its holders.
The difference between returns on its assets and the interest it pays on reserve balances.

These features help explain why central banks have traditionally earned profits. They often hold interest-bearing assets while issuing currency that does not pay interest and reserve balances that may carry a lower interest rate than their assets.
Although central banks generally operate separately from government fiscal authorities, they are public institutions and usually transfer a substantial portion of their profits to the government. Governments also maintain accounts at their central banks: tax receipts can be deposited into these accounts, and government payments can be made from them.
Their income includes interest on loans to banks, interest on securities, gains or losses from financial trading, and fees. Their expenses include interest paid on reserves as well as staff costs, currency production, and other operating expenses.

section: 3.4 Can a Central Bank Become Insolvent?
text:
3.4 Can a Central Bank Become Insolvent?
Under a commodity-backed monetary system, such as the gold standard, a central bank may promise to convert its currency into a specified amount of gold or another asset at an agreed exchange rate. In that case, maintaining sufficient assets to honour the conversion commitment is important.
Under a modern fiat money system, by contrast, central bank currency is generally not redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or other assets. In the sense discussed in the lecture, the obligation represented by currency in circulation is therefore largely notional: the central bank has no promise to redeem banknotes for a particular physical asset.
Consequently, a fiat-money central bank can, in an accounting sense, have negative capital—its assets may be worth less than the monetary liabilities recorded on its balance sheet—without necessarily experiencing the same kind of insolvency crisis as a commercial bank.
The purchasing power of fiat currency is reflected in the price level: what a unit of currency can buy. As emphasized in the lecture, it is not mechanically determined by the book value of the assets held by the central bank.
This does not imply that central banks can acquire risky assets without consequences. Sound asset management and risk-control procedures remain important for at least two reasons:

Opportunity cost. If a central bank purchases a low-return or unnecessarily risky asset, it forgoes the return it might have earned on a more attractive alternative. That foregone income could otherwise have been transferred to the government.
Indirect costs through inflation. Monetary expansion can, under some circumstances, contribute to inflation and reduce the purchasing power of money. This creates a potential social cost even if the central bank does not face an immediate accounting constraint.

The central bank therefore needs to manage the risks associated with assets acquired through money creation, even though central bank solvency is not equivalent to commercial bank solvency.

title: 3  Central Banks
text:
3.5 Functions of Central Banks

3.5.1 Monetary Policy
Monetary policy refers to the policies implemented by a central bank to influence monetary and financial conditions in the economy. Open market operations are one instrument of monetary policy.
In traditional textbook models, monetary policy is often presented as control over the quantity of money issued by the central bank, whether in the form of currency or reserves. Over recent decades, however, major central banks have generally focused less on directly targeting monetary aggregates and more on influencing interest rates, especially the rates at which households, firms, and financial institutions borrow and lend.
Central banks use their ability to create reserves, together with their operating frameworks and policy instruments, to influence market interest rates. The lecture indicates that later material will explain why interest rates have become the principal operational focus of monetary policy and how the Federal Reserve and the ECB implement their policies.


3.5.2 Lender of Last Resort
A bank may experience a liquidity crisis when depositors or other creditors withdraw funds rapidly. If the bank lacks sufficient liquid assets to meet these withdrawals and cannot obtain funding from other banks or financial markets, it needs an alternative source of liquidity.
In practice, this emergency financing role is often performed by the central bank, which acts as the lender of last resort.
There are several reasons why governments may prefer central banks to perform this function:

Money-creation capacity: A central bank can provide emergency liquidity by creating and crediting reserves to a commercial bank’s account.
Greater confidentiality and speed: Central bank lending may be arranged more discreetly than direct government support, which may require public debate or legislation.
Different fiscal treatment: Central bank lending is not ordinarily recorded as direct government expenditure.

Because of this role, central banks are often given an explicit responsibility for financial stability.


3.5.3 Banking Regulation and Supervision
It is important to distinguish banking regulation from banking supervision:

Banking regulation refers to the rules that banks must follow, including capital adequacy and liquidity requirements.
Banking supervision refers to the process of monitoring and assessing whether banks comply with those rules. Supervisors may also evaluate corporate governance and risk-taking practices and, in extreme cases, revoke a bank’s operating licence.

There is an ongoing debate about whether central banks should be directly responsible for banking supervision. One concern is that supervisory objectives might conflict with monetary policy objectives, such as price stability. For example, a central bank could face difficult trade-offs between tightening monetary conditions to control inflation and protecting a fragile banking system.
An opposing view, supported by the lecturer, is that participation in banking supervision helps central banks understand financial conditions, conduct monetary policy more effectively, and carry out their lender-of-last-resort responsibilities.
The lecture also discusses the ECB’s role in the euro area’s Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM).


3.5.4 Public Finances and Monetary Financing
Central bank money creation may generate income that can ultimately benefit the government, particularly when a central bank earns profits and transfers them to the fiscal authorities. Historically, revenue associated with money issuance has been an important fiscal resource in some circumstances.
Some proponents of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) argue that a government issuing its own currency has considerable capacity to finance expenditure through monetary arrangements, subject ultimately to real resource and inflation constraints. In simplified accounts of this approach, taxes may be used to reduce private-sector purchasing power when the economy is overheating.
Similar ideas predate MMT. In the 1940s, Abba Lerner developed the concept of functional finance, which emphasizes evaluating fiscal policy according to its macroeconomic effects rather than treating a balanced budget as an end in itself.
In practice, however, many modern economies maintain institutional separation between central banks and fiscal authorities, and impose legal or operational restrictions on direct monetary financing of government expenditure. These arrangements reflect concerns that excessive reliance on monetary financing could:

Encourage governments to depend too heavily on money creation.
Generate excessive inflation.
Undermine central bank independence.
Subordinate monetary policy to the government’s financing needs.

The distinction is therefore between the technical capacity to create central bank money and the institutional, legal, and macroeconomic constraints on using that capacity to finance public spending.

title: 4  The Fed and the ECB
text:
4.1.1 The Federal Reserve
The Fed was founded in 1913, and its legal framework has evolved substantially since then.
Historical evolution

Initial purpose — lender of last resort. The Fed was originally created primarily to supply liquidity to the banking system during crises and thereby reduce the risk of bank runs and financial panics.
Problems during the Great Depression. Despite this original purpose, the Fed did not adequately prevent the banking difficulties of the 1930s.
Institutional reform and a broader policy role. With the development of the modern Board of Governors in Washington, D.C., and greater banking stability after the 1930s, monetary policy gradually became its central responsibility.
Renewed focus on banking stability. More recent financial crises have once again highlighted the importance of financial stability and banking supervision.

The Fed’s principal legal foundation is the Federal Reserve Act, as subsequently amended. The Act identifies several objectives:

A high level of employment.
Stable prices, meaning low and stable inflation.
Moderate long-term interest rates.

The first two objectives are commonly emphasized as the Fed’s dual mandate. Nevertheless, moderate long-term interest rates also appear in its statutory objectives.
Economic interpretation: Monetary policy may confront trade-offs between employment and inflation in the short run. The Fed’s mandate requires it to consider both macroeconomic outcomes rather than treating price stability as the only legally specified objective.


4.1.2 The European Central Bank and the Eurosystem
The legal foundation for the euro area’s single monetary policy was established by the Maastricht Treaty (entering into force in 1993).
It is important to distinguish the ECB from the entire monetary-policy system:
Eurosystem = ECB + national central banks of euro-area countries.
The Eurosystem has a clear hierarchy of objectives.
Primary objective: price stability
The Treaty states that the primary objective is to maintain price stability. Unlike the Fed’s multiple statutory objectives, the ECB’s primary objective is explicitly given priority.
Secondary objectives: support broader economic policies
Without prejudicing price stability, the Eurosystem is also required to support broader economic objectives. The lecture identifies these as including:

A high level of employment.
Sustainable, non-inflationary growth.
Competitiveness.
Convergence of economic performance among member countries.

The qualification “without prejudice to price stability” is crucial: support for employment and growth must remain consistent with the ECB’s primary objective.
Inflation target
The lecture describes the ECB’s current strategy at that time as aiming for 2% inflation over the medium term. An earlier formulation was “below, but close to, 2%.” The newer formulation places 2% at the centre of the objective rather than making an inflation rate just below 2% the preferred outcome.

4.2 Organisation and Decision-Making Bodies

4.2.1 The Federal Reserve System
Two institutions must be distinguished:

The Federal Reserve System is the entire central-banking system.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) makes the principal monetary-policy decisions.

The Federal Reserve System consists of:

The Board of Governors, based in Washington, D.C.
12 regional Federal Reserve Banks, distributed across the United States.

Together, these institutions perform central-banking functions, including currency-related operations and the management of payment systems. Many operational responsibilities are decentralised to the regional Reserve Banks.

4.2.1.1 The FOMC
The FOMC has 12 voting members:

The seven members of the Board of Governors.
The President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Four presidents from the remaining regional Reserve Banks, with voting seats rotating among them.

The Chair of the Board of Governors also chairs the FOMC. The New York Fed President serves as the FOMC’s Vice Chair. In the 2025 lecture, these officeholders are identified as Jerome Powell and John Williams, respectively.
The FOMC ordinarily meets eight times per year, although additional emergency meetings can be arranged when necessary.
New York has a central role in U.S. financial markets and in the implementation of open market operations. It is therefore institutionally distinct from other regional Reserve Banks in the FOMC’s voting structure.


4.2.1.2 Geography of Federal Reserve districts
The map shows that the boundaries of the twelve Federal Reserve districts reflect the distribution of the U.S. population around 1913**.






Figure 4.1: Twelve Federal Reserve districts



This historical structure matters because:

Population and economic activity were more concentrated in certain eastern and midwestern regions when the Fed was established.
The South and West subsequently expanded substantially.
The district structure nevertheless retains its historical boundaries.

Thus, the geographic structure of the Fed does not simply reproduce the present-day distribution of population or economic activity.



4.2.2 The ECB and the Eurosystem
The ECB is run on a day-to-day basis by its six-member Executive Board. The lecture identifies Christine Lagarde as the ECB President.
The main monetary-policy decision-making body is the Governing Council, which comprises:

The six Executive Board members.
The governors of the participating NCBs.

The Autumn 2025 slides describe 20 participating NCB governors, giving the Governing Council 26 members at that time. Its monetary-policy meetings are normally held every six weeks at the ECB’s headquarters in Frankfurt, with an annual meeting hosted elsewhere in the euro area.

4.2.2.1 National central banks remain active participants
Membership in the monetary union does not mean that an individual NCB simply disappears or is fully replaced by the ECB.
For example, the Central Bank of Ireland no longer determines an independent interest-rate policy for Ireland, but its governor participates in the formulation of monetary policy for the euro area as a whole.
NCBs also perform important operational functions:

Implement many of the Eurosystem’s monetary-policy operations.
Carry out currency-related functions.
Operate payment systems.
Produce economic statistics and forecasts.
Monitor public finances and other domestic economic developments.

The Eurosystem therefore has a highly decentralised operational structure. Activities that might be performed primarily by a central board in Washington are often distributed across national central banks in the euro area.

title: 4  The Fed and the ECB
text:
4.3 Political Independence and Accountability
Central bank independence means that monetary-policy decisions can be made without direct political interference. Accountability means that an independent institution must still explain its decisions and answer to democratically constituted bodies.
These concepts are related, but they are not identical: independence does not imply an absence of accountability.

4.3.1 Political independence of the Fed
The Fed enjoys important operational independence:

Its monetary-policy decisions do not require approval by Congress.
The President cannot directly veto individual FOMC policy decisions.

However, the Fed’s independence has institutional limits:

Congressional authority. Congress can amend the Federal Reserve Act and potentially change the Fed’s mandate or institutional design.
Political appointments. Members of the Board of Governors are appointed through the U.S. political process.
Length of tenure. Governors have statutory 14-year terms, designed to reduce the influence of short-term political pressures. A governor appointed to complete a predecessor’s unfinished term may in practice serve a shorter period.
Chair appointment. The Chair serves a four-year term as Chair, even while holding a longer-term position as Governor, and may need reappointment to continue in the leadership role.

Under the Humphrey-Hawkins framework, the Fed provides Congress with semiannual monetary-policy reports, including its assessments and projections of economic activity and inflation. The Fed Chair also appears before congressional committees to testify and answer questions.
Fed’s independence is relatively limited by international standards.


4.3.2 Political independence of the ECB
The ECB was designed to possess a particularly high degree of institutional independence.
Its protections include:

Treaty-based mandate. Its key objectives are entrenched in European treaties, making them much harder to amend than ordinary national legislation.
Long, non-renewable Executive Board terms. Executive Board members serve eight-year terms and cannot be reappointed. This limits incentives to please politicians in order to secure another term.
Minimum terms for NCB governors. National central-bank governors must have terms of at least five years.
Euro-area-wide responsibility. Governing Council members are expected to decide according to the interests of the euro area as a whole, not the interests of their home countries.
Prohibition on political instructions. European treaty provisions prevent political authorities from seeking to direct ECB monetary-policy decisions.

Executive Board appointments involve agreement among the participating countries’ political leaders, but once appointed, board members are protected by the ECB’s independence framework.
The ECB must:

Prepare an annual report for the European Parliament.
Have its President appear four times per year before the Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs.

The ECB has strong legal and political protections for independent policy decisions, while maintaining reporting and hearing obligations at the European level.


4.3.3 Independence from fiscal authorities
An important danger for monetary stability is fiscal dominance: a situation in which fiscal financing needs constrain monetary policy, potentially pressuring the central bank to create money to cover government deficits.
Historically, monetary financing of fiscal deficits has contributed to episodes of high inflation. The euro-area framework contains explicit safeguards against this risk.

4.3.3.1 Article 123 and monetary financing
Article 123 of the European treaty framework prohibits the ECB and national central banks from:

Extending overdrafts or comparable credit facilities to governments and specified public-sector institutions.
Directly purchasing debt instruments from those public-sector issuers.

The crucial distinction is between primary-market and secondary-market government-bond purchases.








Operation
Who sells the bonds to the central bank?
Treatment in the lecture

Government issuing the bonds
Prohibited for ECB/NCBs; direct Treasury purchases also prohibited for the Fed


Purchase in the secondary market
An existing investor or another market participant
Permitted, subject to the applicable rules



The ECB’s Asset Purchase Programme (APP), one form of quantitative easing (QE), involved government-bond purchases in secondary markets. The Fed can similarly purchase Treasury securities in secondary markets.
Why does this distinction matter? Buying a newly issued bond directly from a government provides funds to the issuer immediately. Buying an existing bond from an investor changes the portfolios and liquidity of financial-market participants instead. This legal distinction enables monetary-policy asset purchases without authorising unrestricted direct financing of budget deficits.

text:
4.4 Banking Supervision
Banking supervision involves monitoring the safety and soundness of financial institutions. It is related to, but distinct from, setting policy interest rates.

4.4.1 Banking supervision in the United States
The U.S. system is characterised by multiple supervisory authorities, rather than one single regulator.
The lecture highlights three institutions:







Institution
Role emphasised in the lecture




Federal Reserve
Supervision of major bank holding companies


Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
Supervision of national banks


Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC)
Supervision of smaller state-chartered banking institutions in the lecture’s simplified description



A bank holding company is an entity that owns or controls banks. Supervision at the holding-company level allows regulators to consider risks affecting the wider banking group.

4.4.1.1 Effects of the global financial crisis
Following the 2008 global financial crisis, the Fed’s role in financial supervision expanded, particularly under the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010.
The lecture identifies three changes:

Thrift supervision: The Office of Thrift Supervision was abolished, and the Fed acquired supervision of thrift holding companies. Thrifts are savings-oriented financial institutions, historically associated with housing finance.
System-wide oversight: The Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC) was established to monitor threats to financial stability. The Fed participates in this interagency council and has a significant role in banking-system stress tests.
Certain non-bank institutions: The Fed was given supervisory responsibilities for non-bank financial firms whose safety and soundness were considered important to the wider financial system, following FSOC designation.

Main lesson: After the crisis, the Fed’s supervisory responsibilities increasingly reflected concerns about systemic risk, not just the safety of individual banks.



4.4.2 Banking supervision in the euro area
Historically, different euro-area countries organised supervision differently:

Some relied on their national central banks.
Others used independent supervisory agencies.

This diversity created a challenge for a common monetary area: financial distress in one member state could have consequences elsewhere, even though supervision remained fragmented.

4.4.2.1 Development of the Single Supervisory Mechanism
In June 2012, euro-area leaders agreed on a framework allowing the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), the common financial-assistance fund, to support undercapitalised banks. A key accompanying institutional step was the creation of common euro-area banking supervision.
The ECB assumed its role in the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in late 2014.
According to the 2025 course slides, the ECB then directly supervised 119 banks, accounting for more than 80% of euro-area banking assets. These figures should be read as the lecture’s reported statistics, not as live supervisory totals.
The SSM operates through a division of responsibilities:

Significant banks: Supervised directly by the ECB.
Other banks: Generally supervised by national competent authorities.
ECB oversight: The ECB may assume direct supervision of another credit institution when necessary to ensure consistent supervisory standards.

Before taking over, the ECB conducted a comprehensive assessment of the banks within its direct supervisory remit. It also cooperates with the European Banking Authority (EBA) on stress testing.
A stress test asks whether a bank would remain adequately capitalised if it suffered a severe adverse economic or financial shock.
Main lesson: The SSM moved euro-area banking supervision toward a common framework, although national authorities still carry out substantial supervisory work.

title: 4  The Fed and the ECB
text:
4.5 Lender of Last Resort
A lender of last resort provides emergency liquidity when financial institutions face serious funding pressures. This role is especially important when a liquidity crisis threatens to spread through the financial system.
It is useful to distinguish two problems:

Illiquidity: An institution cannot obtain sufficient cash or immediately usable funds to meet payments as they fall due.
Insolvency: An institution’s assets are insufficient to cover its liabilities, so liquidity support alone may not repair the underlying problem.


4.5.1 6.1 Lender of last resort: the Fed

4.5.1.1 The discount window
The Fed operates a discount window through which eligible banks can borrow from the central bank when needed. The lecture emphasises that borrowing banks are normally expected to be in generally sound financial condition.
The discount window therefore provides a standing channel for central-bank liquidity assistance to banks.


4.5.1.2 Emergency lending under Section 13(3)
Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act provides a broader emergency-lending authority, enabling the Fed to extend support beyond traditional bank borrowers in exceptional circumstances.
During the 2008–2010 financial crisis, the Fed used emergency facilities to:

Support funding in disrupted financial markets.
Prevent the failure or disorderly collapse of important financial institutions.
Reduce the transmission of financial distress across the economy.

Although these interventions helped stabilise the financial system, they were politically controversial.


4.5.1.3 Restrictions following the crisis
The lecture notes subsequent restrictions, including:

Emergency lending under Section 13(3) requires approval from the U.S. Treasury Secretary.
The Fed may no longer use Section 13(3) to make firm-specific rescue loans of the type associated with the crisis; the emergency facilities are instead subject to broader eligibility requirements.
Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA) provides a separate framework for resolving certain failing financial firms. The lecture notes that its effectiveness had not yet been tested in practice as of the lecture date.

Key distinction: Emergency lending addresses funding problems, whereas orderly liquidation is a mechanism for dealing with institutional failure. They are related responses to crises, but they are not the same intervention.



4.5.2 Lender of last resort: the ECB / Eurosystem
The Eurosystem provides bank liquidity through:

Regular refinancing operations, including weekly operations.
A marginal lending facility, which eligible banks may use to borrow from the central bank when necessary.

These loans require eligible collateral, meaning assets that satisfy the Eurosystem’s requirements for securing central-bank credit.

4.5.2.1 Why can collateral become a constraint?
During a severe funding crisis, a bank may exhaust its available eligible collateral. Even if central-bank borrowing facilities exist, the bank may be unable to borrow enough because it has no additional acceptable assets to pledge.
At that point, the bank may seek Emergency Liquidity Assistance (ELA).


4.5.2.2 Emergency Liquidity Assistance
The lecture describes the ELA framework as follows:

National central banks provide ELA. The relevant NCB undertakes the lending and bears the associated credit risk.
ECB oversight remains important. The ECB’s Governing Council can restrict or stop ELA when a two-thirds majority determines that the programme interferes with Eurosystem objectives.
ELA can create difficult judgments. Authorities must distinguish between a bank that is fundamentally viable but illiquid and a bank whose losses may already have made it insolvent.



4.5.2.3 Historical controversies
The slides discuss several disputes involving ELA during the 2010s:

Possible insolvency: ELA was sometimes extended to banks that appeared to be insolvent.
Ireland, Cyprus, and Greece: The ECB’s power to restrict ELA influenced the timing and design of EU–IMF financial-support programmes.
Anglo Irish Bank: Repayment of ELA by failed, nationalised banks contributed to significant costs for taxpayers.
Cyprus (2013): Some depositors suffered losses after emergency liquidity had helped finance withdrawals by better-informed depositors.

These cases show that lending-of-last-resort decisions may have major distributional, fiscal, and political consequences.

Takeaway: The lender-of-last-resort function requires more than the technical ability to create central-bank money. It also requires legal authority, acceptable collateral, judgments about solvency, and a clear allocation of financial risk.

title: 4  The Fed and the ECB
text:
4.6 Monetary-Policy Meetings

4.6.1 How FOMC meetings work
The Fed publishes full FOMC meeting transcripts after a five-year delay, making it possible to study the deliberations in considerable detail.
The lecture describes a typical sequence:

Staff briefings: Officials present recent developments in financial markets, the U.S. economy, and the international economy.
Macroeconomic forecasts: Participants discuss staff projections for economic growth, employment, inflation, and related variables.
Regional roundtable: Reserve Bank presidents describe economic conditions in their own districts, bringing local information into national policy deliberations.
Break: The meeting may pause before moving to policy recommendations.
Chair’s assessment and proposal: The Chair presents a preferred policy action and proposes wording for the FOMC’s public statement.
Discussion and vote: Participants debate and vote on the proposal. Members who disagree may register a dissent and briefly explain their reasoning.


4.6.1.1 Why does statement wording matter?
A central bank affects the economy not only through its current interest-rate decision but also through expectations about future policy.
The FOMC statement can therefore influence market expectations even when the policy rate itself remains unchanged. This helps explain why the Chair’s proposed wording is an important component of the meeting.



4.6.2 How ECB Governing Council meetings work
Since 2015, the ECB has published written accounts of Governing Council monetary-policy meetings.
These accounts describe:

Information provided to policymakers about economic and financial developments.
The general nature of the policy discussion.

However, the accounts generally do not attribute particular comments to named participants.
The ECB’s voting transparency also differs from the Fed’s:

Policy decisions were historically often presented as unanimous.
Disagreements do occur, but individual voting results are not routinely released.
As the lecture notes, it may not always be clear whether a formal vote occurred.


4.6.2.1 Rotation of national central-bank voting rights
The euro area’s expansion required a system that would allow participation without making the number of voting members excessively large.

section: 4.7 Communication with the Public and Markets
text:
4.7 Communication with the Public and Markets
Central-bank communication is an important part of monetary policy because households, firms, and financial markets make decisions partly on the basis of expected future interest rates and economic conditions.

4.7.1 Communication by the Fed
After each FOMC meeting, the Fed publishes an official statement setting out:

The monetary-policy decision.
Its assessment of economic and financial conditions.
Its views about inflation risks.
The voting outcome, including dissenting votes where applicable.


4.7.1.1 Evolution of Fed transparency

Before 1994: The FOMC did not issue a statement after its meetings.
Before 1999: Statements were generally released only when the target federal funds rate changed.
More recently: The statements have become longer and more informative, often discussing expected policy settings and asset purchases.

The Fed also publishes detailed minutes several weeks after its meetings, while full transcripts are released after a five-year lag.
Beginning in 2011, the Fed Chair started holding press conferences after selected FOMC meetings. Under Chair Powell, press conferences became a regular feature after every scheduled meeting.
In addition, FOMC participants communicate through public speeches and congressional testimony.


4.7.1.2 Forward guidance
Statements about how long interest rates may remain low, or how the central bank plans to purchase assets, provide information about its expected future policy path.
This is commonly described as forward guidance. The lecture highlights how the wording of statements became especially important during periods when short-term interest rates were near zero.



4.7.2 Communication by the ECB
After each Governing Council monetary-policy meeting:

The ECB issues a monetary-policy statement.
The ECB President reads and explains the statement at a press conference.
Journalists question the President about the policy decision, country-specific developments, and complex policy programmes.

The statement explains the decision with reference to the ECB’s announced monetary-policy strategy.
ECB press conferences illustrate the practice of central-bank-speak: highly deliberate, technically precise language intended to avoid sending unintended signals to financial markets.
The President generally tries to remain “on-message”, meaning consistent with the Governing Council’s agreed communication strategy. However, unclear wording or an unexpected response can still create market confusion and volatility.
The ECB also makes press-conference transcripts and webcasts available online, and Governing Council members regularly give public speeches.


4.7.3 Why communication is economically important
Monetary policy influences financial conditions through at least two channels discussed in these notes:

The current policy decision, which affects short-term funding conditions.
Information about expected future policy, which can influence expectations and financial-market pricing.

Therefore, a central bank’s statement, minutes, press conference, and public speeches can be policy-relevant even when no immediate change is made to its interest-rate target.

title: 5  Banking Crises
text:
5.1 Banking Crises and Their Consequences
We have discussed how the banking system works and the role that banks play as financial intermediaries during “normal times.” Over the next few weeks, we are going to cover banking crisis. We will focus on how and why they happen, on how governments attempt to prevent them, and on policy options for dealing with them when they occur.
We will cover these topics in the following order:
Banks generally make profits by charging higher interest rates on loans than they pay out on deposits. But things can go wrong sometimes. Sometimes, borrowers don’t pay back their loans or the other assets invested in lose much of their value. Banks can also sometimes make bad investments in other assets such as stocks or bonds.
What if a bank makes losses so that its assets go below what it owes to depositors and bond-holders, i.e. it has negative equity capital?

title: 5  Banking Crises
text:
5.1.1 Insolvency and Bank Runs
Once it is suspected a bank is insolvent, if depositors fear that they may not get their money back, this can trigger a bank run: Depositors line up to demand their money back.
In September 2007, depositors of Northern Rock, who had limited deposit insurance from the UK government, started to take their money out of its branches. This was the first time since the 1930s that advanced economies saw retail bank runs of this type. More recently, a number of US banks (most notably Silicon Valley Bank) experienced bank runs in which customers withdrew their deposits online.
The bank can start paying off depositors by selling off its most liquid assets, e.g. cash, excess reserves at the central bank, government debt securities. But once those assets are gone, the bank will have to start selling assets that are not liquid and so not easy to quickly turn into cash, e.g. long-term customer loans or property assets.
Selling off non-liquid assets quickly (an asset fire-sale) often requires having to sell the assets for less than if they had been sold in a more orderly manner. The bank run triggered by its insolvency ends up making the bank even more insolvent—the value of its assets fall even farther behind liabilities.
Sometimes a bank run can be triggered by mere rumours that the bank is insolvent. Even if the rumours are false, the bank may still end up being insolvent if it has to sell its assets quickly at a discount to pay back its liabilities. For this reason, bankers and governments are always quick to declare that banks are fully solvent. Even if they are not so sure, the bank and the government will want to prevent a run.


5.1.2 Contagion
On its own, a single bank failing and some depositors losing some money is unfortunate but not necessarily a major concern. However, once one bank fails, it can often put other banks under pressure.
If one bank has lost money on a particular type of loan or security investment, how can depositors be sure that other banks are not also about to lose similar amounts?
To depositors, two banks with similar loan portfolios probably look the same.
If one has lost plenty of money and is insolvent, how can we be sure that the other isn’t heading in the same direction? Northern Rock’s problems were triggered by US banks with similar-looking business models getting into trouble rather than clear problems with the value of its assets. Indeed, two banks with similar names may seem similar to the public.
So bank runs can be contagious: After one bank fails, depositors start to look for their money back from other banks. Bank failures thus tend to come together in batches. The banking system may seem healthy one minute and then suddenly the whole system becomes unstable.


5.1.3 Implications of Banking Crises for Credit
Banking crises usually lead to severe restrictions on the availability of credit to firms and households. To see why, let’s look at a stylized balance sheet and think about what happens during a banking crisis:



Assets (Uses of Funds)
Liabilities (Sources of Funds)




Cash and Reserves
Deposits


Securities
Other Borrowings


Loans
Equity Capital



By definition Loans = Deposits + Other Borrowings + Equity Capital - Cash and Reserves - Securities.
Banking crises see movements in deposits, other borrowings, and bank cash and securities holdings, all of which lead to a lower quantity of loans.

Deposits: If some customers lose faith in banks and prefer to keep cash in a mattress, then banks will have less funds to loan out.
Other Borrowings: Similarly, bond markets and other providers of funds may be less willing to lend to banks that they worry may fail.
Cash and Reserves: To survive potential runs on the banks, they will keep larger amounts of cash and reserves for precautionary reasons.
Securities: Even when money is invested, banks will shift towards securities that can be quickly sold to raise cash.

The result is a reduction in loans. It’s hard for banks to “call in” existing loans but when loans are paid off, banks will keep the funds as cash or reserves or invest in securities instead of making new loans or use them to pay off deposit outflows or maturing bond liabilties.
So both bank and customer behaviour contributes to a credit crunch: Banks are no longer in a position to lend to borrowers and financial intermediation breaks down.


5.1.4 Macroeconomic Effects of Banking Crises
Financial intermediation is crucial for economic activities like house purchases, car purchases, starting a new business and so on. When banking crises happen, banks stop playing their crucial role as financial intermediaries and the economy suffers: Sectors such as housebuilding and consumer durables suffer particularly badly.
Without access to credit, business and consumer confidence suffers and this has further negative effects on the economy. For these reasons, banking crises can be hugely damaging, triggering severe recessions. We know that the global financial crisis of 2007/2008 triggered a severe worldwide recession but this was not the first time.
Ben Bernanke was Fed Chair during the 2008/09 financial crisis. His early research (long prior to joining the Fed) had focused on the role played by the banking crisis in worsening the Great Depression of the 1930s. Here are some quotes from a
.

The banking problems of 1930-33 disrupted the credit allocation process by creating large, unplanned changes in the channels of credit flow. Fear of runs led to large withdrawals of deposits, precautionary increases in reserve deposit ratios, and an increased desire by banks for very liquid or rediscountable assets. These factors, plus the actual failures, forced a contraction of the banking system’s role in the intermediation of credit.
As the real costs of intermediation increased, some borrowers (especially households, farmers, and small firms) found credit to be expensive and difficult to obtain. The effects of this credit squeeze on aggregate demand helped convert the severe but not unprecedented downturn of 1929-30 into a protracted depression.



5.1.5 Additional Complications in Modern Banking Crises
Modern banking systems have a number of additional features that make banking crises more difficult to deal with than in the past.

Non-Deposit Funding: While deposit insurance tends to reduce the chance of retail bank runs, many modern banks obtain substantial non-deposit funding via bond markets or inter-bank money markets. These providers of funds are more prone to “run” than depositors, who are often viewed as a “sticky” source of funding.
Interbank Linkages: Funding links between banks can mean that the failure of one bank can directly threaten the failure of other banks.
Financial Assets and Negative Feedbacks: Many banks now have very large holdings of financial assets, whose valuations (unlike loans) are set in the market every day. During crises, we can see negative feedback loops involving banks selling assets, which then decline in value, thus making bank solvency problems even worse.

These additional complications led to a range of government interventions during the global financial crisis of 2008/09, many of which were expensive for taxpayers.

5.1.5.1 Why More Non-Deposit Funding?
A common feature of the modern financial system is that many banks now rely heavily on non-deposit sources of funding. There are a number of reasons for this.

Deepening of Financial Markets: Modern financial systems contain more options than in the past for people to channel their savings towards. Two that are relevant for banks are pension funds, which commonly buy bonds issued by banks and money market mutual funds, which commonly make shorter-term loans to banks.
Financial Globalisation: In closed economies, savings must equal investment. Banks that are provided with savings from depositors must make loans within their own country. In an open economy, savings do not need to equal investment. In a country that has high savings but low investment, banks will often lend funds to banks in other countries. In pre-crisis Europe, banks in countries with current account surpluses (like Germany) provided lots of funds for banks in countries with current account deficits (e.g. Ireland, Portugal, Greece).
Deregulation: Regulations about where banks get funds from, and who they can loan these funds to, have generally been loosened over time.



5.1.5.2 Modern Bank Runs: Non-Deposit Funding
Problems with failing banks in recent years have rarely involved depositors getting jittery and withdrawing money: Modern bank runs mainly come from those who lend money to banks through interbank markets and bond markets deciding not to continue supply a bank with funds.
Non-deposit funding is much less “sticky” than deposit funding. Those who provide it are more likely than depositors to check on the bank’s situation and pull money at the first sign of trouble.
Northern Rock may have looked like an exception but it actually wasn’t: The depositor runs happened well after other lenders to the Rock had begun to pull money. Only after the Bank of England announced emergency support did retail depositors realise what was going on.
Much of Northern Rock’s funding was in the form of “securitised notes”: These were bonds backed by the mortgages issued by Northern Rock as collateral in case the bank defaulted. When doubts about Northern Rock’s business model emerged, its non-deposit funding quickly tailed off.
Non-branch-related deposits also left the bank very quickly.


5.1.5.3 Interbank Lending and Systemic Risk
Interbank markets make it easier for banks to cope with reserve requirements (by lending and borrowing short-term funds) and allowing banks with lots of deposits but without good loan opportunities to lend to banks with good loan opportunities but limited deposits. But they can also contribute to making the banking system unstable.
Consider the following example:

Three banks (A, B and C) all have equity capital of €10 million.
Bank A has borrowed €25 million from Bank B and Bank B has borrowed €15 million from Bank C.
Now suppose Bank A loses €35 million in bad property loans. This wipes out its equity capital. The bank becomes insolvent and is wound up and Bank B does not get its €25 million back.
Bank B is now insolvent and cannot pay back the €15 million it owes Bank C. This means that Bank C also has no equity capital and so is insolvent.

Bank A going down brings the whole system down. This example describes what is known as systemic risk.


5.1.5.4 Asset Price Fire Sales and Spillovers
The previous example is not very realistic. It required the first bank to lose an amount that wasn’t just greater than its own capital but an amount greater than the capital of the whole system. But we have left out another important channel through which one bank getting in trouble affects others.
When banks get into trouble and start selling liquid assets (stocks, bonds, etc) in a hurry to pay off depositors or lenders—often termed a fire-sale of assets—this places downward pressure on the prices of these assets.
Modern banking regulations have required banks to “mark their tradeable assets to market” as much as possible. So if the failure of one bank leads to the prices for some financial assets falling, then other banks have to mark down the value of their assets also.
The asset price fire sales reduce the equity capital of other banks and place them under threat. A single bank failure can lead—via contagion and spillovers from asset sales—to the whole system becoming unstable.



5.1.6 The Bank-Sovereign “Doom Loop”
The euro area crisis of 2011/12 illustrated a new form of systemic risk: The interaction between banks and governments.
The global banking crisis saw many European banks receiving support from their national governments. In some cases, such as Ireland, the extent of this support undermined the confidence of financial markets in the confidence of governments. Weakness in the banking sector spread to the sovereign.
But euro area banks also had large (and increasing) holdings of their own country’s sovereign debt, so a sovereign debt default (as occurred in Greece) would threaten the solvency of the banks. Weakness in the government sector spread to the banking system.
Banks in countries with weak fiscal situations were also more likely to experience runs because depositors and investors would think the state was unable to provide funds for a bail out or for recapitalisation.
This created a sort of “doom loop” in which weaknesses in different parts of the system fed upon each other. In a June 2012 statement, the Euro Area leaders said “We affirm that it is imperative to break the vicious circle between banks and sovereigns.” Some progress has been made but elements of this loop still exist.
