title: 5  Banking Crises
text:
5.2 The Global Financial Crisis of 2008/09






Figure 5.2: Depositors queue outside Northern Rock during the 2007 bank run.




5.2.1 The Roots of the Crisis
The early 2000s was an era of unprecedented low interest rates around the world. Low mortgage rates made it easy to borrow more money to buy houses. This produced a huge boom in house prices and many countries (such as Ireland, Spain and the US) had big housing construction booms.
In the US, there was a boom in sub-prime mortgage lending (i.e. borrowing by people with poor credit records). This was largely financed by securitisation: Banks would bundle together a set of mortgages and use their repayments to provide the income flows for securities that would be purchased by investors.
These mortgage-backed securities (MBS) were risky. If people defaulted on the mortgages, then the investors who bought these securities would lose money.
Despite the risks, the MBS were purchased by financial institutions all over the world. Why did banks and other investors buy sub-prime MBS given the risks involved?

Confidence in House Prices: There was recognition of higher default risk but confidence that high and rising house prices would mean no losses when units were foreclosed (repossessed).
Geographic Diversification: MBS were backed by mortgages from all over the US. There had been regional house price booms and busts but the modern era had not seen simultaneous falls in house prices all over the country.
Credit Ratings: Many of the MBS—even many of those backed by subprime mortgages—had been rated AAA by ratings agencies, so they seemed safe.
Fraud: Many of the subprime mortgage applications featured incorrect or fraudulent documentation of salaries, property values, owner occupancy and second liens. It is not clear how much investors knew.
The Great Moderation: Macroeconomic fluctuations since the mid-1980s had been much smaller. People believed they were living in a “great moderation” period with limited macroeconomic risk.



5.2.2 House Prices Fall and Delinquencies Start
Eventually, anything that is unsustainable has to stop. Subprime mortgage origination peaked in 2005 and by 2006, with mortgage rates rising and some evidence mounting of the poor credit quality of recent loans, the financing boom ended.
With prices already out of line with reality and the funding boom over, house prices began to fall in Spring 2006, slowly at first and then quickly. Not only were many people who took out mortgages unable to pay them back but soon many of them were in negative equity.
Many US states have “non-recourse” mortgages: You can give the keys back to the bank and tell them to take the house (so-called “jingle mail”), so the bank takes a loss if the house is sold for less than the value of the mortgage.
Investors, in particular, were happy to just walk away. Even when banks do have recourse to pursue the debts, the legal process is slow and expensive.
Rather than supplying a steady stream of repayments to service the MBS, many of these mortgages became “salvage operations” as the mortgage server repossessed the houses and hoped to sell them for as much as possible.
Quickly, there was an unprecedented wave of delinquencies.
Over 2008, investors began to realise the riskiness of banks around the world.

Risk Exposure:

Many global banks (particularly European banks) had purchased large quantities of MBS.
Some of the banks that were selling the MBS also ended up holding large amounts of their own products in 2008.
Many leading banks were also engaged in lots of proprietary trading activity. With markets falling, there was the risk of large losses.

Capital and Funding Weaknesses

Leading banks were highly leveraged, with insufficient capital to absorb large losses.
The heavy reliance on short-term non-deposit funding end up triggering a series of liquidity crises.








Figure 5.3: Bank capital ratios and reliance on short-term funding before the global financial crisis.





5.2.3 The Policy Response: Pre-Lehmans
The first seeds of the crisis became evident in August 2007 as doubts grew about the implications of losses on subprime MBS for various financial institutions. From August 2007, the Fed, ECB and Bank of England greatly stepped up their liquidity providing operations as banks considered vulnerable began to lose funding.But very little was done to address the solvency problems of major international banks, which lay at the heart of the crisis.
Over the first year, the global response to the crisis was somewhat ad hoc.

In August 2007, the UK authorities were slow to help Northern Rock, because of concerns about moral hazard. They only stepped in to nationalise the bank after a full-scale run had taken place. Northern Rock shareholders lost all their money.
In March 2008, there was a non-deposit run on Bear Stearns. JP Morgan bought Bear Stearns with the US government insuring them against the losses on Bear’s mortgage-backed security portfolio.
In early September 2008, MBS issuers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac were put into conservatorship.



5.2.4 The Lehmans Decision and the Aftermath
By September 2008, the US authorities felt the previous bailouts had been politically unpopular and had set a bad precendent. So, when Lehman Brothers investment bank suffered the same kind of non-deposit run that Bear Stearns had, the Fed and the US Treasury made the decision to not help and Lehmans filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008.
Financial markets panicked.
Faced with uncertainty about which institutions could survive to pay back their debts and which couldn’t, many financial markets effectively collapsed in the weeks and the months after Lehman brothers bankruptcy saw the world economy plunge into its worst recession since the 1930s.
Around the world, authorities decided that they simply could not afford to let any more banks fail for fear of further disruptions. The US quickly passed the Troubled Assets Relief Programme bill, a $700 billion package of measures to restore stability to the banking system. Other countries also passed emergency measures.






Figure 5.4: The LIBOR–OIS spread during the global financial crisis.









Figure 5.5: Bank stock prices by country during the global financial crisis.





5.2.5 Why Did It Become a Global Banking Crisis?
Why did the US subprime crisis turn into a global banking crisis?
One answer is because of the exposure of European banks through their holdings of subprime MBS. However, losses on MBS represented only a small fraction of the equity of European banks.
There wer other, more indirect, channels that lead investors to pull their funds from banks.

Complexity: The complexity of MBS and the widespread use of off-balance sheet vehicles to purchases these securities made it difficult to identify the exposure of counterparties to subprime. This led to a generalized retreat from lending and risk.
Short-Term Funding: Reliance on short-term funding such as repo or asset-backed commercial paper was also widely used in the European banking system. The US crisis exposed the fragility of this model.
Reassessment of Risk: Beyond the exposure to subprime, the US crisis exposed many bad practices that were also in use at European banks such as excessive leverage, excessive dependence on credit ratings, inadequate risk management and lax oversight by supervisors.



5.2.6 A Severe Global Recession
The period after the Lehman Brothers failure saw the most severe global recession since the Great Depression. The recession had three principle drivers.

Direct Effects of Falling House Prices: As the value of people’s homes declined, households spent less money. The “home equity release” source of money disappeared. House construction collapsed as it became much less profitable.
Debt Crisis: Governments, businesses and households that had taken on large amounts of debt prior to the crisis had to tighten their belts. This led to reduced consumption spending, less business investment and fiscal austerity.
Financial Conditions: It is well known that financial sector weakness exacerbates recessions. Banks were required to reduce the size of their balance sheets and this lead to big declines in lending to households and firms.

Due to trade and financial linkages, the whole world ended up being severely affected by this recession. However, the recession was larger in advanced economies, most likely due to their greater reliance on large financial systems.

title: 5  Banking Crises
text:
5.3 Bank Failure and Resolution

5.3.1 The Need to Intervene Early on Failing Banks
Banking supervisors could hold off on intervening on a weak bank until it is clear to the public that the bank has major problems. But there are important reasons to intervene prior to that point.

Firstly, it is important to avoid panic and possible contagion.
Secondly, failing banks can cause serious problems. Bankers who know their bank is failing but are not reporting the true figures have an incentive to “gamble for resurrection” by seeking out highly risky investments with a potentially high upside. History is littered with stories of bank executives engaging in highly risky or even illegal behaviour in order to save their bank or else prevent the public from seeing its true state. These actions can end up having a serious impact on the bank’s creditors by raising the total amount of losses and may also cost the taxpayer if the bank’s creditors are bailed out because of deposit insurance or other guarantees.

Financial supervisors thus usually intervene early either to demand a recapitalisation of the bank or, if that is not possible, to shut the bank down.


5.3.2 Who Loses When a Bank Fails?
Consider the stylized balance sheet:



Assets (Uses of Funds)
Liabilities (Sources of Funds)




Cash and Reserves
Deposits


Securities
Debt Securities (Bonds)


Loans
Equity Capital



A bank that is insolvent has negative equity capital: It does not have sufficient assets to pay back its liabilities. So who loses out?
Shareholders in the wound-up bank get nothing (though there is a hierarchy between common and preferred equity, with regular shareholders losing first).
What about other claims? Who loses out among depositors and bond holders? Some bonds (“senior bonds”) come with contracts claiming they rank equally (“pari passu”– Latin for “equal footing”) with depositors. If there are only enough funds to pay out 80 percent on deposits and senior bonds, then senior bonds get 80 cents for each dollar owed.
However, there is no requirement for government deposit insurance to make up for the missing 20 cents that bondholders lost.


5.3.3 Subordinated Bonds
Some bonds, known as subordinated bonds, rank behind senior bonds and deposits. If the bank is wound up, these bond-holders will only get their money back if there is money left after assets have been sold off to pay off the depositors and senior bond-holders.
Here’s an example of the legal rights of a subordinated bond holder, in this case an AIB “Perpetual Preferred Security.” “The obligations of the Guarantor under the Subordinated Guarantee will rank junior as to payments to all liabilities to creditors of the Guarantor (including without limitation depositors, general creditors and subordinated debt holders) and claims of holders of senior ranking securities. In the event that the Guarantor is wound-up, liquidated or dissolved, the assets of the Guarantor would be available to pay obligations under the Subordinated Guarantee only after all payments have been made on such senior liabilities and claims.”
Why would someone purchase a bond that could lose out if the bank is wound down? Higher interest rates. To compensate for the additional risk, they yield a higher return and some investors are happy to take this risk.


5.3.4 Dealing with Insolvent Banks: Bank Resolution
Often, before the bank actually publishes a report admitting to being insolvent, supervisors seize the bank and begin the process of using its the assets to pay off its creditors, i.e. the people it owes money to. This process is often referred to as bank resolution.
If these assets do not cover the value of deposits, then the deposit insurance fund can be used to compensate the depositors. This occurs particularly often in the US, where there are many banks and the FDIC seeks to avoid having insolvent banks abuse the deposit insurance cover that they provide. See the “failed bank” list on the website for a list of banks that the FDIC has closed this year.
In an extreme case, the bank is wound up and depositors are sent cheques.
More common is the purchase and assumption approach. The FDIC arranges for another bank to take on the deposits and provides it with funds to make up for the shortfall in assets required to cover these liabilities.
Another common approach to bank resolution is to split the bank into a “good bank” and a “bad bank” with the bad bank taking on both lower-ranked liabilities and having lower-quality assets.

title: 5  Banking Crises
section: 5.4 Policies to Prevent and Deal With Banking Crises
text:
5.4 Policies to Prevent and Deal With Banking Crises

5.4.1 Preventing Crises: Deposit Insurance
One potential solution to banking instability is government deposit insurance: The government guarantees the depositors money.
If depositors know their money is fully covered by the government, they won’t turn up in large numbers looking for their money back. This can act to prevent the kind of damaging bank runs that afflicted the US banking system in the 1930s.
After the Great Depression, deposit insurance was introduced into the US. The deposit insurance scheme is run by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and is financed by a charge on banks covered by the insurance. Even if a bank fails, most depositors would get all their money back, with shortfall due to bank insolvency being covered by the deposit insurance fund. Deposit insurance has since spread around the world and retail bank runs are now rare.
Note that deposit insurance operates separately from any pari passu clauses for bank liabilities. A bank that is put into liquidation inflicts losses on depositors as well as senior bondholders. The government then makes up for losses incurred by depositors.

5.4.1.1 Problems with Partial Deposit Insurance
Prior to the global financial crisis of 2008/09 many governments had only partial insurance schemes in place. For example, in Ireland, the government used to just insure 90% of deposits up to a maximum of €20,000.
These partial insurance schemes don’t really prevent bank runs. A similar partial insurance scheme existed in the UK and failed to prevent the depositor run on Northern Rock. Who wants to lose even 10% of their money? And most deposits come from big depositors so limits on insurance means most of their money will still be at risk.
After the financial crisis, many governments made deposit guarantee schemes more generous, raising maximum amounts and eliminated the “partial” element of insured deposits.

In the US, deposits in individual accounts are now fully insured up to $250,000 and people can have multiple insured accounts. But this didn’t stop a run on SVB, who had large amounts of uninsured deposits from clients such as technology firms.
EU members all now provide full deposit insurance up to €100,000.



5.4.1.2 Risks Due to Deposit Insurance
Deposit insurance schemes can help by acting to prevent deposit runs, which are one of the key triggers for banking crises. However, there are a number of downsides to such schemes.
In the absence of any risk of losing their money, depositors won’t spend any time monitoring the riskiness of the lending being taken by their banks.
And banks can now take big risks with their loans, knowing the government will bail out depositors if things go bad. This may encourage the bankers to take greater risks: One could argue that they are gambling with the state’s money.
This issue is known as the moral hazard problem and it applies to all types of insurance: Once you know insurance against certain behaviour is in place, you may be more likely to engage in this behaviour.
There is evidence that deposit insurance in developing countries made banking systems less stable. And banking system bailouts tend to be very expensive.



5.4.2 Lender of Last Resort Policies
Even with deposit insurance, banks can still run into liquidity problems so that they are having trouble meeting outflows. As we discussed before, a key role of central banks is to act as a lender of last resort to banks. If banks cannot get loans from elsewhere, then the central bank can provide them with one.
But what policies should a central bank follow in providing these kinds of loans?
Usually, central banks follow the recommendation set down in 1873 by English journalist Walter Bagehot:

To avert or contain panics, central banks should lend freely to solvent institutions, against good collateral.

Since 2008, both the Fed and ECB have provided large amounts of “last resort” lending to banks. However, the ECB’s procedures in relation to Emergency Liquidity Assistance are unclear and decision-making have seemed arbitrary and sometimes politicised.
These central bank liquidity programs undoubtedly helped to contain the various banking crisis since 2008 but they are not without controversy.

5.4.2.1 Controversy over The Lender of Last Resort Function
Earlier we discussed the need for central banks to carefully assess the risks they need to take when creating money. This means they need to be careful when loaning money to banks during crises.
If a bank is really insolvent and only has poor quality collateral, then effectively public money is being used to compensate the bank’s private creditors. One can question whether this is a good use of public money.
And, as we have noted before, it can be hard to distinguish during a crisis between liquidity and solvency problems.
For these reasons, deciding on the terms and quantity of last resort lending can be a difficult policy decision. In 2007, Bank of England Governor Mervyn King was very reluctant at first to lend exceptional amounts to Northern Rock, citing “moral hazard” concerns (i.e. that it would set a bad precedent and encourage other banks to be less carefully managed.)
In the euro area, there has been lots of controversy over the ECB Governing Council’s approval of ELA to distressed banks and the process of emergency loans has often been politicised. We will discuss this in greater detail later.



5.4.3 How Should Governments Respond?
The problems discussed here—unstable uninsured non-deposit funding, large holdings of financial market assets, and the inter-connected nature of the financial system—have posed serious questions for policy makers responding to banking crises.
One of the first question governments need to ask about whether a bank should be let fail (i.e. introduce bank resolution and see that uninsured creditors lose money) is whether this institution is of systemic importance. Would the bank’s failure lead to the whole financial system becoming unstable? Is the bank “too big to fail”?
On the other hand, governments need to be careful about insuring banks simply because they are big:

Large banks may turn out to be “too big to save”. For example, the Irish state was unable to rescue its banks without ruining the government’s credit rating and requiring an EU-IMF bailout.
Bailing out large banks that are too big to fail presents another kind of moral hazard problem: Will large banks take more risks knowing the government can pay off their creditors if the risks don’t pay off?

When faced with a bank that is in serious trouble, governments can choose between bank resolution methods (protecting insured deposits and seeing that other creditors lose out) or intervene by using public funds to pay off uninsured creditors such as bond holders.
When making this decisions, governments usually have two considerations in mind:

Would the failure of the bank represent a source of systemic risk? If the failure of the bank to pay back its creditors will lead to the failure of other banks and a systemic banking crisis, then the government may decide it has to guarantee uninsured creditors.
Moral Hazard: Alternatively, governments may worry that providing state guarantees to uninsured creditors will encourage these investors to be reckless with their money, knowing that the government will always bail them out. Guaranteeing these creditors will likely encourage further crises and raise the cost of the required bailouts.



5.4.4 Responses to the 2008 Crisis: Non-Deposit Guarantees
The global banking crisis of late 2008 saw non-deposit funding from large institutional investors (pension funds, money market mutual funds, other banks) fleeing from banks.
Governments all across the world intervened to help banks continue availing of non-deposit funding. Many countries gave state backing to new borrowings from banks so that these banks could continue to access medium and longer-term funding.
A more extreme case: On 30 September 2008, Ireland gave an almost blanket state guarantee to all the liabilities of our six main banks. This meant that, if these banks were unable to pay back their bond market borrowings, the Irish government were going to pay them back on behalf of these banks.

Two of the banks guaranteed that night—Anglo Irish Bank and Irish Nationwide—turned out to be deeply insolvent.
The final cost of paying off creditors at Anglo Irish Bank and Irish Nationwide Building Society was about €36 billion.

Page 14 of Patrick Honohan’s report

“As regards the substance of the guarantee itself, it is hard to argue with the view that an extensive guarantee needed to be put in place, since all participants (rightly) felt that they faced the likely collapse of the Irish banking system within days in the absence of decisive immediate action. Given the hysterical state of global financial markets in those weeks, failure to avoid this outcome would have resulted in immediate and lasting damage to the economy and society. There would have been additional lost income and employment surely amounting, if it could be quantified, to tens of billions of euros. Nevertheless, the extent of the cover provided (including to outstanding long-term bonds) can – even without the benefit of hindsight – be criticised inasmuch as it complicated and narrowed the eventual resolution options for the failing institutions and increased the State’s potential share of the losses.”


Page 128: “The inclusion of existing long-term bonds and some subordinated debt (which, as part of the capital structure of a bank is intended to act as a buffer against losses) was not necessary in order to protect the immediate liquidity position. These investments were in effect locked-in. Their inclusion complicated eventual loss allocation and resolution options.”



5.4.5 Other Responses: Bad Banks, Insurance, Equity Injections
Other state responses to the banking crises included:

State-Funded Recapitalisations: After the Lehman Brothers collapse in 2008, governments around the world put state funds into banks to recapitalise them, taking shares for the state but usually on generous terms for the banks (who were reluctant to admit they need funds and don’t want to take them from the state.) US Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP) was originally intended to purchase assets (as in the NAMA approach) but quickly became a scheme to add equity to the leading US banks.
State Asset Management Agencies: Another way to reduce uncertainty is to move the assets into a government-owned agency (e.g. Irish NAMA plan). If buying from private banks, it may require over-paying for the assets to get the banks to participate.
Asset Insurance Schemes: The UK government provided insurance to banks such that in return for a fee, the UK government agreed to cover loan losses above a certain amount. This reduced the uncertainty of potential losses for banks but exposed the UK taxpayer to large downside risk.

title: 5  Banking Crises
text:
5.5 Bank Resolution in Europe
Due to concerns that the global financial crisis of 2008/09 placed too much burden on taxpayers, a new approach to dealing with failing banks was introduced.
The Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive (BRRD) was introduced in 2015, providing a new “single rulebook for the resolution of banks and large investment firms”.
BRRD set up a new body, the Single Resolution Board (SRB) with various powers to deal with banks that are “failing or likely to fail” These powers include

A “bail-in” tool, allows the write-down of debt owed by a bank to creditors or its conversion to equity.
The power to enforce FDIC-style “purchase and assumption” deals.

In 2017, Banco Popular of Spain was declared “failing or likely to fail”. Shareholders and subordinated bondholders lost their money. The bank was sold to another bank (Santander) for one euro. Depositors were protected and no state money is used.

title: 6  Incentive Problems in Banking
text:
6.1 Example
Why do banks get into trouble sometimes?
Our traditional image of a banker is of someone who is very conservative and risk-averse. Can’t we rely on the self-interest of conservative bankers to ensure that most banks maintain sufficient equity capital and that bank failure will be a rare event?
The answer is no. It turns out that the incentives of bank management can lead them to take risks that sometimes end up getting their banks into trouble.
We start by discussing how the personal financial incentives of bank executives can lead them to run banks that are too leveraged (i.e. too little equity capital relative to assets), have too many risky investments, and have too much short-term non-deposit funding.
In the language of microeconomics, the bankers do not take into account the negative externalities generated by their behaviour. Negative externalities of this sort are a classic example of when government intervention can improve economic outcomes. In this case, there is an argument for government regulation of the banking sector.
We’ve discussed how banking works via a simple balance sheet listing assets and liabilities. To better understand how banks work, we’re going to go through a little exercise in which we imagine setting up a bank and figuring out what a bank CEO gets up to.
Let’s start with the assumption that the bank is founded by a bunch of investors who have €10 million. Then they hire you to run the bank for them. They expect you to make as much money for them on their investment as you can. Let’s see how it goes.

title: 6  Incentive Problems in Banking
section: 6.3 Incentives of Bank Shareholders and CEOs
text:
6.3 Incentives of Bank Shareholders and CEOs
These calculations show why we can’t rely on bankers self-interest to maintain sufficient capital to protect against losses. The higher credit and liquidity risk means higher bank profits.
There are two different elements to consider here:
Investor Incentives: People differ in how much risk they are willing to take. Shareholders of a highly-leveraged bank may be willing to accept a risk of losing all their money in return for a high return most of the time. Maybe by the time the bank blows up, they will have made a nice return from all the dividends the bank has paid back.
Bank CEO Incentives: Even if the bank’s shareholders don’t want to take on a lot of risk, there are strong incentives for bank CEOs to operate with high leverage. Profit-linked bonuses are very important for senior bank management, so they want to maximize profits today. If the bank blows up next year, they don’t have to pay the bonuses back. So they have an incentive to take big risks while pretending to shareholders that they are being prudent.

6.3.1 Incentives to Take Excessive Risk in Lending or Investment
We have seen how banks may be incentivised to have too much leverage. For a given amount of equity, a bank with more assets will generally deliver a higher return on equity. For bank CEOs, the higher returns from more leverage may matter more than the smaller probability that credit or liquidity risks bring down the bank.
Similar arguments apply to risky lending or investments. Consider an investment that has a ninety percent probability of delivering a 50% return and a 10% probability of losing all your money. A banker who takes on this risk will generally do well and may earn good bonuses. Occasionally, however, his bank will become insolvent. He may decide it’s worth the gamble.
Sometimes bankers get into trouble because everyone believes a certain type of investment (technology stocks, housing) is a “one-way bet” and only realise too late that they are wrong.
Why don’t the bankers question the prevailing wisdom? Often, the money being made is just too good. Also, recall Keynes’s comment:

“A ‘sound’ banker, alas! is not one who foresees danger and avoids it, but one who, when he is ruined, is ruined in a conventional and orthodox way along with his fellows, so that no one can really blame him.”



6.3.2 Incentives to Rely on Short-Term Debt
By September 2007, it was clear that some major banks were going to incur large losses that would threaten their solvency. Many of them had funded their operations with very short-term borrowing, which began to flow out.
See paper by Diamond and Rajan:

“Given the complexity of bank risk-taking, and the potential breakdown in internal control processes, investors would have demanded a very high premium for financing the bank long term. By contrast, they would have been far more willing to hold short-term claims on the bank, since that would give them the option to exit – or get a higher premium – if the bank appeared to be getting into trouble.” In other words, they took this option because it was cheap.

Vanity Fair article on Bear Stearns

“By midafternoon the dam was breaking. One by one, repo lenders began to jump ship. As word spread of the withdrawals, still more repo lenders turned tail …. A full $30 billion or so of repo loans would not be rolled over the next morning. They might be able to replace maybe half that in the next day’s market, but that would still leave Bear $15 billion short of what it needed to make it through the day … By four o’clock the firm’s reserves, which had been $18 billion that Monday, had dwindled to almost nothing.”







Figure 6.3: Bear Stearns’ Cash Holdings, February 22–March 13, 2008 (billions of dollars).





6.3.3 Incentives to be Too Big
Previously, we discussed the idea of systemic risk, i.e. how a bank may be perceived as “too big to fail” because its failure can bring down the whole financial system.
This provides an incentive for banks to grow bigger in size over time: The bigger they are, the more likely the state will intervene to save them if things go wrong. In addition to being highly leveraged (high ratio of assets to equity) this can also be achieved by taking over other banks or seeking new equity investments.
In 2009 paper from November 2009 titled “Banking on the State” Piergiorgio Alessandri and Andrew Haldane of the Bank of England documented how banking sectors had grown in size relative to the economy, had become more leveraged and less liquid, and had engaged in more risky trading activities.
Some quotes from the paper are on the next few pages.

“Gains to shareholders are potentially unlimited. But the same is not true in bad states of the world. The reason is limited liability. That constrains the losses of shareholders to around zero. Losses beyond that point are borne by other parts of banks’ capital structure - wholesale and retail depositors. Therein lies the problem. If protection of depositors is felt to be a public good, these losses instead risk being borne by the state, either in the form of equity injections from the government (capital insurance), payouts to retail depositors (deposit insurance) or liquidity support to wholesale funders (liquidity insurance). The gains risk being privatised and the losses socialised. Evidence suggests this is a repeated historical pattern.”


“Socialised losses are doubly bad for society. Taxes may not only be higher on average. They may also need to rise when they are likely to be most painful to taxpayers, namely in the aftermath of crisis. So taxes profiles will be spiky rather than smooth and will spike when the chips are down.”


“So far, so bad. But it is about to get worse, for this tells only half the story. This is a repeated game. State support stokes future risk-taking incentives, as owners of banks adapt their strategies to maximise expected profits. So it was in the run-up to the present crisis.”

Alessandri and Haldane: The Doom Loop

“These strategies are the latest incarnation of efforts by the banking system to boost shareholder returns and, whether by accident or design, game the state. For the authorities, it poses a dilemma. Ex-ante, they may well say ‘never again’. But the ex-post costs of crisis mean such a statement lacks credibility. Knowing this, the rational response by market participants is to double their bets. This adds to the cost of future crises. And the larger these costs, the lower the credibility of ‘never again’ announcements. This is a doom loop.”



6.3.4 Incentive Problems with MBS
We described before how poorly performing subprime mortgage-backed securities (MBS) played a key role in the global financial crisis of 2008/09. This crisis was partly due to various parties having incentives that aligned badly with the MBS being of good quality.
Appraisers: Many mortgages came with reports appraising the properties as having higher value than they were worth. The banks making the loans (the originators) wanted reports showing the houses had high value (to make the loan-to-value ratios lower, so the mortgage seemed safer). So to keep getting business, appraisers inflated valuations.
Originators: The banks that made the original loans would then sell these mortgage assets to the underwriters, large investment banks that would bundle the mortgages together and create the MBS. They made money off fees from the originators and cared about those fees, not whether the mortgages were poor quality.
Underwriters: They made money from selling the MBS to investors and did not always care much about the quality of the product.
Ratings Agencies: These got paid by the underwriters and so they had incentives to claim the MBS were safer than they actually were.

title: 6  Incentive Problems in Banking
text:
6.4 The Need for Regulation
We have seen how, left to make their own decisions, bankers will chose to take too much risk. This means that banking crises are not just unfortunate accidents that are an unhappy by-product of the fractional reserve banking system.
Rather, most banking crises stem from bankers making decisions that prioritise their short-run profits over the long-run stability of the banking system and the economy. This means that banks need to be regulated by the government.
We will discuss banking regulation next.

title: 7  Micro-Prudential Banking Regulation
text:
7.1 Basel Accord
micro-prudential，意思是监管目标主要放在单个银行是否稳健，而不是整个金融体系的系统性风险。后者通常叫 macro-prudential regulation，宏观审慎监管。
微观审慎的重点是 资本充足率规则，即要求银行持有足够资本，避免资产规模相对于资本过大，也就是避免过度杠杆。让银行有足够“缓冲垫”吸收损失，保护存款人和高级债权人。
银行业务是全球性的，如果各国监管规则差异太大，会导致监管套利。例如银行可能把业务转移到监管更宽松的国家。因此，从 1988 年 Basel Accord，巴塞尔协议 开始，国际银行监管形成了共同框架。
Basel 框架把可吸收损失的资本分为两类：
监管资本 = Tier 1 capital + Tier 2 capital
其中 Tier 1 capital 更重要，因为它更接近真正意义上的银行自有资本。
Basel 的逻辑是：资产越风险，银行越需要更多资本。所以不是简单要求银行资本等于总资产的某个比例，而是先把资产按照风险加权，得到 RWA，risk-weighted assets，风险加权资产。

text:
7.2 Basel II
Basel II 的主要变化有三点：

风险桶更细 根据评级机构评级区分风险，例如 AAA 债务风险权重低于 AA 债务。
允许大银行使用内部评级法 IRB IRB 是 Internal Ratings Based approach，即银行用自己的风险模型评估资产风险。
抵押贷款被认为比 Basel I 假设的更低风险

Basel II 让资本要求更贴近真实风险，但即使 Basel II 完全实施，也无法阻止 2008 年全球金融危机，甚至可能让情况更糟。为了说明Basel II的缺陷。

7.2.1 IRB
IRB 是 Basel II 中允许大银行使用的一种内部模型方法。它的目标不是处理银行“正常情况下已经预期到的损失”，而是确保银行有足够资本来应对意外损失。

例如，如果银行预期某类贷款中有 1% 会无法收回，那么这 1% 应该一开始就通过贷款损失准备 provisioning 从贷款价值中扣除，而不是依靠资本来吸收。
IRB 的核心逻辑是：用统计模型构造“非常糟糕但可能发生”的情景，然后根据这些情景计算资产的风险权重，再由风险加权资产 \(RWA\) 推出资本要求。也就是说，资本要求不再简单取决于资产类别，而是更精细地取决于模型估计出来的风险水平。但监管者不能完全让银行自由选择模型，因为银行有动机通过模型设定来压低风险权重，从而降低资本要求。因此 Basel 2 规定了模型框架，银行可以选择部分参数，但底层模型结构由监管规则提供。
对大多数银行而言，最主要的风险是信用风险，即借款人无法偿还贷款。IRB 方法从银行自身历史数据和统计模型出发，为每笔贷款估计三个关键参数：PD、LGD 和 EAD。

Loss Given Default，违约损失率
一旦违约，银行预计损失的贷款比例


EAD
Exposure at Default，违约风险暴露
违约发生时银行面临风险的贷款金额



然后，IRB 根据这些参数计算每笔贷款的风险权重，并由此得到风险加权资产：
\[
RWA = EAD \times Risk\ Weight
\]
最低资本要求为：
\[
Capital\ Requirement = 0.08 \times RWA
\]






Figure 7.2: Credit loss distribution: expected, unexpected and stress losses.





7.2.2 VaR
除了信用风险，银行还面临市场风险，即可交易证券如股票、债券等因市场价格波动而发生损失。VaR 的逻辑是估计银行投资组合损失的概率分布。
这里使用的核心工具是 Value-at-Risk，VaR，风险价值。VaR 衡量的是：在给定持有期和置信水平下，银行交易组合可能遭受的最大预期损失。例如，10天持有期、99%置信水平下的 VaR 可以理解为：

在正常模型假设下，有 99% 的概率，未来10天损失不会超过这个数值；但仍有 1% 的概率损失会超过它。

例如，如果银行的每周 VaR 是 5000 万美元，意思是：在未来一周内，只有 1% 的概率损失会超过 5000 万美元。
注意VaR 不告诉你最坏情况下会损失多少，它只告诉你某个概率分位点。
银行通常使用市场价格、波动率和相关性等历史数据来计算 VaR。Basel 对 VaR 计算设定统一框架，包括：通常使用10天持有期、99%置信水平、至少一年历史市场数据，并要求进行压力测试。
银行需要根据交易账户的 VaR 计算市场风险资本要求。资本要求取以下两者中的较高者：

最近一期 VaR，也就是 current-day VaR；
过去60个交易日每日 VaR 的加权平均值，即 average VaR；

然后再乘以监管设定的 scaling factor，通常为 3。
监管者还要求银行进行 backtesting 回溯检验，即比较模型预测的 VaR 与实际交易损失。如果银行模型持续低估风险，监管者可以施加额外惩罚或提高资本乘数。此外，Basel 还要求银行在普通 VaR 之外补充 Stressed VaR，sVaR，用来衡量历史高压力时期，如高波动、相关性失效时期，可能发生的损失。最终市场风险资本要求由 VaR 和 sVaR 共同构成。

title: 7  Micro-Prudential Banking Regulation
section: 7.3 Risks and Problems with Capital Requirements
text:
7.3 Risks and Problems with Capital Requirements
VaR 在理论上简单，但实际操作中问题很多。主要有两个问题：

估计样本问题：VaR 通常基于历史数据估计损失分布。但历史样本不一定代表未来。例如 2005—2007 年金融市场看起来很平稳，如果银行只用这段数据估计风险，会得出很低的 VaR。但 2008 年危机马上爆发，说明这些估计严重低估了风险。
尾部风险问题：VaR 只关心某个分位点，比如 99% 分位点，却不关心最坏 1% 情况下究竟会损失多少。金融市场常常有 fat tails，厚尾分布，极端损失发生频率高于正态分布预测。因此，用正常分布估计 VaR 很可能低估危机中的真实损失。

瑞士央行前行长Philipp Hildebrand 对 Basel II 的批评

While sensible, the higher risk sensitivity of Basel II comes at a price. First, banks and supervisors alike incur significant operational costs to implement the new, highly complex regulation. Second, but in my view more importantly, Basel II creates new risks: Risks about risk assessments. I am tempted to call them the unknowable unknowns. Under Basel II, we increase our dependence on risk models. What if we didn’t pick the correct models? What if the data used to calibrate these models turn out to be of poor quality? What if the models were correct in the past, but the future is different? What if certain tail events simply cannot be modelled? These are all important considerations that we have to keep in mind when we interpret the risk figures from complex models. As it turns out, to view the model outputs as a true representation of reality has proven to be a grave mistake.”

因此过度相信复杂模型是一种严重错误。监管不能只依赖银行内部模型。
Northern Rock的例子进一步说明 Basel II 的问题。Northern Rock 在 2007 年6月30日的报告说：

The implementation of Basel II results in our Pillar I risk weighted assets at 30 June 2007 falling from around £33.9 billion under Basel I to £18.9 billion under Basel II, a reduction of some 44%. The risk weighting for our residential mortgages reduces to mid-teens %, treasury assets to around half of Basel I requirements, also around mid teens %, reflecting the low risk nature of these portfolios and personal unsecured loans to slightly below Basel I requirements.

这意味着在 Basel II 下，银行被认为风险更低，因此所需资本减少。管理层甚至认为这是好消息，并提高股息。但几个月后，Northern Rock 陷入严重危机，最终被国有化。
这个案例说明：模型计算出的低风险不一定是真实低风险。资本要求下降可能反而鼓励银行增加分红、提高杠杆，而不是增强稳健性。






Figure 7.3: Risk-based capital ratios of surviving and failed major global banks, end-2006.




7.3.1 非对称风险
Asymmetric risk positions，非对称风险头寸指这样一种资产：

大多数时候产生小额稳定收益；
极少数时候产生巨大损失。

我们看下边两个例子：

7.3.1.1 选择 A：普通风险投资
每天可能赚 10 万，也可能亏 10 万。收益波动比较明显。

这种投资的损失经常出现，所以 VaR 很容易捕捉到风险。银行模型会发现：这个资产经常亏钱，风险不低。


7.3.1.2 选择 B：非对称风险投资
大多数时候赚小钱，极少数时候亏巨款。

现在看起来非常诱人：

99.5% 的时候都赚钱；
日常收益非常稳定；
历史数据里可能很少出现亏损；
VaR 可能显示风险很低。

但真正的问题是：一旦进入那 0.5% 的灾难状态，亏损不是 10 万，而是 1 亿。
而银行为了激励经理人，可能不仅奖励他们赚钱，还奖励他们“低风险地赚钱”。例如奖金规则可能是：
\[
奖金 = 利润 / VaR
\]
因为银行希望员工不是单纯追求利润，而是追求风险调整后的利润。在这种情况下，经理人就有动机选择看起来 VaR 很低但实际上有巨大尾部风险的头寸。典型例子是信用违约互换 CDS credit-default swap。可以把 CDS 理解成一种针对债券违约的保险。

平时债券不违约，收取小额保费；看起来收益稳定、风险很低；
但一旦金融危机爆发，大规模违约同时发生，损失巨大。

VaR 可能看不到这种极端尾部损失，因为它只关注 99% 以内的情况，而忽略最坏 1% 情况中损失规模有多大。AIG 在危机前大量出售 MBS 相关 CDS，最后陷入破产并由美国政府救助，这就是典型例子。
UBS 在2008年的经济危机中，由于持有了大量美国次贷 MBS 而遭受巨大损失。
Patrick Honohan 对 UBS 的分析：

Most of UBS’s losses relate to their portfolio of MBS, many of which were being warehoused for sale to other entities. Evidently, the mark-to-market value of these assets fell sharply during 2007. In broad terms, what appears to have happened in respect of at least some of the losses is that insurance and derivatives were bought to hedge only the amount of variation (known to the traders) to which the portfolio was being stress-tested. Market fluctuations larger than envisaged in the stress test were not hedged (otherwise the profit potential of the positions being taken would have been eliminated).
In other words, the profits being booked (in the relevant parts of the business) arose primarily because of – and were the reward for – the assumption of catastrophic risk outside that envisaged in the stress test.
Senior management understood that certain units were taking large positions, but they assumed that the risk models were good enough to protect against serious loss. Perhaps they would have been good enough if not gamed, but they were not perfect, and that they were gamed was perhaps inevitable.

因此风险模型不仅可能不完美，而且可能被内部人员利用。



7.3.2 监管问题
在 Basel II 下，监管者不只是看银行资产，还要：

检查银行的风险暴露；
评估复杂的内部风险模型；
判断模型使用的数据质量；
理解模型假设和输出。

这对监管者来说非常困难，尤其是监管者资源有限，而大型银行模型极其复杂。所以 Basel II 的一个副作用是：监管变得更加依赖银行自己的模型，外部监管者反而更难判断真实风险。
Andrew Haldane 和 Vasileios Madouros 的著名文章 The Dog and the Frisbee批评了越来越复杂的监管规则：

Catching a frisbee is difficult. Doing so successfully requires the catcher to weigh a complex array of physical and atmospheric factors, among them wind speed and frisbee rotation. Were a physicist to write down frisbee-catching as an optimal control problem, they would need to understand and apply Newton’s Law of Gravity.
Yet despite this complexity, catching a frisbee is remarkably common. Casual empiricism reveals that it is not an activity only undertaken by those with a Doctorate in physics. It is a task that an average dog can master. Indeed some, such as border collies, are better at frisbee-catching than humans.
So what is the secret of the dog’s success? The answer, as in many other areas of complex decisionmaking, is simple. Or rather, it is to keep it simple. For studies have shown that the frisbee-catching dog follows the simplest of rules of thumb: run at a speed so that the angle of gaze to the frisbee remains roughly constant

因此，应该重新重视简单、标准化、数量型监管规则。但不能认为简单规则一定总是更好。

title: 7  Micro-Prudential Banking Regulation
text:
7.4 Post-Crisis Banking Regulation
2008 年金融危机后形成 Basel III。Basel III 的主要内容包括：

正常时期 common equity requirement 为 7% 也就是更重视普通股权益资本。
资本保护缓冲 capital conservation buffer 为 2.5% 在压力时期可以动用，但正常时期银行应保持额外资本。
逆周期资本缓冲 countercyclical buffer 为 0—2.5% 当信贷过度增长、系统风险累积时，监管者可以要求银行持有更多资本。
更严格的资本定义 例如对养老金缺口等项目进行更多扣除。
最大杠杆率限制 即限制未加权资产相对于资本的比例，用来弥补过度依赖风险模型的问题。

Basel III 不只是提高资本要求，也加入了宏观审慎色彩，例如逆周期缓冲。
除资本监管之外的，还有其他改革。






Figure 7.4: Capital requirements under Basel II/Basel 2.5 and Basel III.




7.4.1 流动性改革
Basel III 引入：







指标
含义




Liquidity Coverage Ratio, LCR
银行在压力情景下应能承受 30 天资金流出


Net Stable Funding Requirement, NSFR
银行应有足够稳定资金支持一年期资产和业务活动



这说明危机后监管不只关注资本，也关注流动性。


7.4.2 Too Big to Fail
Basel Committee 识别出 28 家全球系统重要性银行，即 G-SIBs。这些银行如果倒闭会威胁全球经济，因此要持有额外 Tier 1 capital，范围大约 1%—2.5%。
Financial Stability Board，FSB，金融稳定委员会。它成立于2009年，由 G20 国家推动设立，任务是负责国际金融监管协调。2015年11月，FSB 对所有 G-SIBs 提出了 TLAC 标准，Total Loss-Absorbing Capacity，总损失吸收能力。TLAC 是指在 G-SIBs 进入处置程序时，可以迅速用于 bail-in 的工具和负债的最低要求。TLAC 的核心思想是：系统重要性银行即使倒闭，也应有足够可以被 bail-in 的债务和资本来吸收损失，而不是由纳税人救助。

7.4.3 分离存款业务和高风险投资
美国 Dodd-Frank Act 中的 Volcker Rule 限制存款机构进行自营交易。英国则引入 ring-fencing，把大银行的存款业务和金融交易业务隔离开。


7.4.4 Basel IV
2017 年后的一轮改革，常被非正式称为 Basel IV。
主要改革包括：

修订标准法 standardised approach 使风险权重更细。例如抵押贷款风险权重取决于 LTV，loan-to-value ratio，贷款价值比。
限制高级 IRB 方法使用范围 某些资产类别不能完全依赖银行内部模型，例如大型企业、银行、其他金融机构敞口。
Output floor，输出下限 银行用内部模型计算的 RWA 不能过低。最终 RWA 至少要达到标准法计算结果的 72.5%。
提高操作风险资本要求

这些改革会使给定资本下的资本比率下降，因为 RWA 被提高了。因此银行可能面临更大增资压力。

title: 7  Micro-Prudential Banking Regulation
text:
7.5 Should Banks Have More Capital?
一个常常讨论的问题是，银行资本要求是否应该更高？
支持高资本的理由很直接：

单个银行更不容易倒闭；
金融系统更稳定；
危机中损失更容易由股东吸收，而不是存款人或政府。

银行家通常反对更高资本要求，原因之一是高杠杆能提高股东回报率。更严肃的反对意见是：权益融资成本高于债务融资，所以更高资本要求会提高银行整体融资成本，进而提高贷款利率。
但这种说法是有问题的。Admati 和 Hellwig 在 The Bankers’ New Clothes 中的观点认为，更高资本要求不一定会显著提高银行整体融资成本。

更高股权资本降低每单位股权风险：如果银行权益资本翻倍，同样一笔损失对每单位股权的冲击会更小。因此股东要求的风险补偿也应下降。
更高资本也降低债务风险。银行更安全，债权人面临违约风险更低，因此债务融资成本可能下降。
Modigliani-Miller 定理根据 MM 定理，企业整体融资成本主要取决于资产风险，而不是债务和股权融资结构。当然现实中 MM 定理有税收、存款保险、政府隐性担保等偏离，但它用于批评“股权更贵所以总体融资成本一定上升”的简单论证。

资本比率有用，但不能完全信任。原因包括：

资本依赖资产估值 如果资产价值被高估，资本也会被高估。
危机中资产价值会迅速下降 资本比率可能在危机前看起来不错，但危机中迅速恶化。
风险加权资本比率未必预测银行失败 Haldane 和 Madouros 认为，危机前的监管资本比率并没有很好地区分哪些银行会失败，简单杠杆率反而预测力稍强。
Banco Popular 案例 Banco Popular 在 2016 年通过 EBA 压力测试，并显示资本充足，但 2017 年进入 resolution。

监管者不能只看公开资本比率，还必须收集其他信息，例如资产质量、流动性、融资结构、治理和风险文化等。

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.1 Financial Cycles: Booms and Crises
Financial historians such as Charles Kindleberger and Hyman Minsky documented historical evidence of how the financial sector tends to go through its own cyclical ups and downs, often involving extreme booms and crashes.
In his famous book “Manias, Panics and Crashes”, Kindleberger describes a financial cycle as follows:
In 1998, famous bond trader Paul McCulley coined the term “Minsky moment” to describe the moment when investors realise the boom is unsustainable and a crash is imminent.
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text: What happens, basically, is that some event changes the economic outlook. New opportunities for profit are seized and overdone, in ways so closely resembling irrationality as to constitute a mania. Once the excessive character of the upswing is realized, the financial system experiences a sort of “distress”, in the course of which the rush to reverse the expansion process may become so precipitous to resemble panic. In the manic phase, people of wealth or credit switch out of money or borrow to buy real or illiquid assets. In panic, the reverse movement takes place, from real or financial assets to money, or repayment of debt, with a crash in the prices of commodities, houses, buildings, land, stocks, bonds—in short, in whatever has been the subject of the mania.
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
section: 8.2 Financial Cycle Mechanisms in Normal Times
text:
8.2 Financial Cycle Mechanisms in Normal Times
Beyond the mechanisms emphasised by Kindleberger that generate major booms and crises, there are some general mechanisms whereby the financial sector and the real economy tend to reinforce each other during normal economic cycles.

Pricing of Risk: The longer an expansion goes on, the more financial market participants start to forget about risk. Risky assets increase in price and risky borrowers receive lower-cost finance.
Asset Prices: These rise during an expansion and provide borrowers with better collateral. With better collateral, banks think borrowers have become a lower risk and borrowers think they can safely borrow more.

The same mechanisms operate negatively on the financial sector during a downturn though often in a more intense fashion than during expansions.
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.3 Financial Cycles and Property Markets
In many cases, property markets are at the centre of pro-cyclical interactions between asset prices and banks.
Banks that are confident property prices will rise may provide loans that fund almost all of the purchase price (or which are a high fraction of the borrower’s income) because they are confident they won’t lose money should the borrower default and the bank repossesses the home.
Rising property prices strengthen the balance sheets of households and firms, who then borrow more money, which further fuels property prices.
When property prices fall, banks make losses on mortgages and cut back on providing credit to the wider economy, perhaps triggering a recession and further reducing property prices.
These points clearly apply to residential property, where most purchases are debt-financed via mortgages, but commercial property booms and busts have traditionally been more dangerous.
Commercial property deals are often speculative and take time to plan and execute. Often, by the time the cycle has turned, investors are left with lots of debt and projects that are no longer economically viable.
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
section: 8.4 Capital Adequacy Rules Can Increase Procyclicality
text:
8.4 Capital Adequacy Rules Can Increase Procyclicality
Micro-prudential capital adequacy rules are intended to keep the banking system stable. But they can have the unintended consequence of making the economy more procyclical.
Consider a bank starting to incur serious losses on its loans and expecting to go below its regulatory capital ratio.
The bank could raise more equity capital by selling shares to private investors. But this would dilute the claim on future dividends of the current owners. And with bank having made recent losses, the cost of equity finance would probably be high.
The other option is to maintain the equity capital at its current level and instead reduce risk-weighted assets. There are two ways to do this:

Reduce Assets. In particular, the bank can use incoming payments from loans to pay off liabilities instead of using them to issue new loans.
Take Less Risk. Invest any new funds in government bonds rather than make potentially risky loans to customers.

These actions can contribute to causing a credit crunch.
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.5 Micro Stability versus Macro Stability?
The point of capital rules are to keep individual institutions solvent. This is why they are termed prudential regulation: They are there to maintain stability by encouraging prudence.
However, rules put in place to encourage each institution to be prudent can add to the self-reinforcing cycles to financial system as a whole, which make it more unstable:

In upswings, we get the following re-inforcing mechanisms:

Asset prices rise, loans are all paid back and this increases equity for banks.
Because of the increase in equity, the regulatory capital rules allow banks to expand their operations by acquiring new assets.
With lots of demand for financial assets, asset prices rise further.








Figure 8.1: Leverage adjustment during an asset price boom.




But booms never go on forever.

Eventually, cycles play out and recession arrives. Then asset prices fall and loans default, eroding equity.
Banks worry about meeting their capital requirements and so they sell off assets.
These sales drive down asset prices and erode equity across the system.








Figure 8.2: Leverage adjustment during an asset price decline.



In an important 2000 paper, Andrew Crockett, former head of the Bank of International Settlements, distinguished between micro-prudential and macro-prudential policy. Here are some quotes.

It follows that the macro-prudential paradigm stresses the possibility that actions that may seem desirable or reasonable from the perspective of individual institutions may result in unwelcome system outcomes. This is a logical contradiction in the micro-prudential vision as defined here. Illustrations of such fallacies of composition are not hard to find. For instance, for a single bank it is only natural to tighten lending standards in a recession, but if all banks do the same the resulting impact on economic activity can lead to a further deterioration in the credit quality of its portfolio. The mirror image during the upswing could generate an unsustainable lending boom, sowing the seeds of subsequent financial instability. Likewise, cutting exposures as market prices fall can deepen the decline in those prices, leading to a drying up of liquidity and exacerbating financial distress.


The quintessential micro-prudential dictum is that “financial stability is ensured as long as each and every institution is sound”. From a macro-prudential perspective, two objections can be levied against this, on the surface, compelling statement. First, it may strive for too much; second, it may deliver too little.
It may strive for too much, because the occasional failure of individual institutions is not the problem. Trying to avoid such outcomes risks providing excessive protection, with the result that market disciplinary and allocative mechanisms are weakened. The statement may deliver too little, because while at one level it is a truism, how the soundness of each individual institution is pursued is crucial. Unless the authorities take into account the impact of the collective behaviour of institutions on economic outcomes, they may fail to monitor risks and take remedial action appropriately.”

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.6 Risk Modelling and Cyclicality
Prior to Basel 2, some academics warned that the use of internal risk models to calibrate risk-weighted assets could exacerbate the procyclicality induced by capital adequacy rules.
Many of the models were estimated using relatively short time windows for calculating risk. During expansion periods, they thought risk was low, during recessions they thought it was high.
Because the risk models told the banks that risk was low during expansions, this meant that risk-weighted assets didn’t increase nearly as much as total unweighted assets.
Banks could increase their leverage during expansions and yet their regulatory capital ratio didn’t show them to be taking big risks.
Again, Andrew Crockett’s paper has a useful alternative way to think about this: “The received wisdom is that risk increases in recessions and falls in booms. In contrast, it may be more helpful to think of risk as increasing during upswings and materialising in recessions.”
crumbs: Central Banks and the Banking System

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.7 What Is Macro-Prudential Policy?
A rough definition: Policies aimed at reducing the financial sector’s procyclical tendencies and making the financial system as a whole more stable (increasing resiliance).
Macro-prudential policies focus on systemic risk rather than risk associated with one or more institution.
From the Central Bank’s macro-prudential policy framework:

The objective of macro-prudential policy is to mitigate the risk of a disruption to the provision of financial services, caused by an impairment of all or parts of the financial system, with serious negative consequences for the real economy. This risk is known as systemic risk.

While there are over-laps between the two parts of this definition—the “reducing procyclicality” and “making the system more stable”—I will briefly mention a number of types of policies under these two headings.

8.7.1 Reducing the Financial Sector’s Procyclical Tendencies

Counter-Cyclical Capital Requirements: This is the classic “macro-prudential” policy. Make banks have higher capital ratios in good times than bad times. Require banks to retain earnings and build up capital during booms and allow lower ratios in recessions.
Regulating the Property Sector: Using limits on mortgages and speculative commercial property borrowing to dampen property-related cycles.
Concentration Limits: Crashes often happen after the financial sector rushes into investing too much in the “next big thing” whether that be property or technology stocks or other asset classes. Limiting exposure to particular sectors, such as commercial property, dampens this kind of excessive concentration.
Monetary Policy: At inflation-targeting central banks, monetary policy is usually set by looking at inflation and the real economy. However, there is an active debate about whether policy rates should be used more actively to “lean against the wind” to reduce credit growth (or “pop bubbles”) during expansions.



8.7.2 Making the Financial System More Stable

More Loss Absorption: The more banks are funded by equity and loss-absorbing bonds, the safer the funding from deposits and senior bonds will be. This reduces the chance of banks runs and all the negative effects they trigger.
Higher Quality Capital: More focus on instruments that can absorb losses while banks keep operating (going concern capital) and less on those that only lose money when banks are liquidated (gone concern capital). Regulators have encouraged the issuance of contingent capital bonds i.e. bonds that turn into equity when capital ratios fall below a trigger level.
Liquidity Regulation: Discourage excessive use of short-term debt and encourage holding of assets less likely to be subject to fire-sale discounts.
Too Big to Fail?: Special regulatory treatment of systemically important banks such as requiring them to have higher levels of capital.
Stress Tests: Regular detailed reporting of how banks would respond to large shocks.

title: 8  Macro-Prudential Policies
text:
8.8 Financial Stability Bodies Around World
Since the global financial crisis, there has been an explosion in new bodies charged with maintaining financial stability and implementing macro-prudential policies.
Edge and Liang (2019) report that only 11 countries had Financial Stability Committees (FSCs) for macroprudential purposes in 2008, whereas 47 countries had FSCs in 2018.
Edge and Liang point out that these committees vary widely in their powers: Some can set capital requirements and put limits on loan-to-value (LTV) rates while others are charged with co-ordinating policy across several different bodies.

8.8.1 An Example: The UK Financial Policy Committee
13 members consist of:

6 Bank of England staff (the Governor, four Deputy Governors and the Executive Director for Financial Stability Strategy and Risk)
external members who are selected from outside the Bank
Chief Executive of the Financial Conduct Authority and one non-voting member from HM Treasury.

Formal description:

Identifies, monitors and takes action to remove or reduce systemic risks with a view to protecting and enhancing the resilience of the UK financial system.”

Informal description (Andy Haldane):

to monitor the punchbowl before it is emptied and before aspirin needs administering.

Powers include the ability to:

Set the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) rate for the UK.
Set sectoral capital requirements for UK financial institutions.
Set a leverage ratio requirement for UK financial institutions.
Set loan-to-value and debt-to-income limits for UK mortgages on owner-occupied properties.
Set loan-to-value and interest cover ratio limits for UK mortgages on buy-to-let properties.



8.8.2 Macro-Prudential Policy in Europe and Ireland

8.8.2.1 Europe:
EU Regulation (1092/2010) established a European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) responsible for the macroprudential oversight of the EU financial system and the prevention and mitigation of systemic risk.
The SSM Regulation (1024/2013) assigns the ECB specific powers in the field of macroprudential policies. It is responsible for assessing macroprudential measures adopted by national authorities in the countries subject to ECB banking supervision.


8.8.2.2 Central Bank of Ireland:
Has “stability of the financial system overall” as an objective under the Central Bank Act.
Is designated by the ESRB as the national macro-prudential authority and is represented on its board.
Is the designated national authority responsible for certain macro-prudential powers in the Capital Requirements Regulation and Directive.



8.8.3 Identifying Financial Stability Risks
Identifying financial stability risks can be tricky.
New regulations and policies are often put in place to deal with the causes of the previous financial crisis (“fighting the last war”, “closing the barn door after the horse has bolted”) but then something new destabilises the system.
Financial Stability committees around the world now issue regular reports devoted to monitoring a wide range of indicators so as not to miss the factors that could trigger the next round of financial disruption.
Many institutions, including the IMF, the ECB and Central Bank of Ireland release regular reports on Financial Stability, .
I have provided links to some of these reports.
Typically, the reports monitor vulnerabilities in the financial system, looking at various sectors such as households, businesses and governments and then review the various policy tools that are available and the options for adjusting them.

title: 9  Money Supply
text:
9.1 Currency and the Monetary Base
In economics, money refers to the most liquid assets—assets that can readily be used to purchase goods and services. Liquidity differs across assets: cash is highly liquid, whereas selling an asset such as a house involves time and transaction costs. Consequently, economists use several monetary aggregates with different degrees of liquidity.
The monetary base and M1 are not the same: bank reserves are part of the monetary base, while checking deposits are included in M1.

title: 9  Money Supply
text:
9.1.1 Central Banks and the Monetary Base
Central banks can control the monetary base.
The monetary base has two components: currency and reserves. One might imagine that currency is the component central banks have the most control over. Central banks are the sole providers of currency, and when they supply it to a bank, they deduct the same amount from the bank’s reserve account.
However, in a modern economy, the amount of currency in circulation is driven by public demand. The Fed or ECB are not going to refuse to provide currency to banks to keep their ATM machines running, provided the banks have sufficient credit in their reserve accounts.
Thus, the way modern central banks control the monetary base is by controlling the quantity of reserves. Reserves can be controlled through open market operations:

Buying securities increases the amount of bank reserves.
Selling securities decreases the amount of bank reserves.



9.1.2 Transaction Usage Does Not Explain Amount of Banknotes in Circulation
Some maths: there are €1,610,000 million in banknotes in circulation, and the euro-area population is estimated at 343 million. That is an average amount of banknotes per person of €4,693.
Pretty clearly, people are not keeping that amount of money on hand for everyday transaction purposes.
Large banknotes (€100 or more) play a much greater role in the supply than one might imagine, accounting for about half the total value of banknotes in circulation.
ECB research, based on information about how often notes are returned to the central bank, estimates that:

Only one quarter of the total value of banknotes in circulation is held for transactional purposes.
Around 30% of the total value of banknotes in circulation is held outside the euro area.
Up to 45% of the value of euro banknotes is held as a store of value (i.e., “mattress money”).

The chart reports that card payments and cash demand have generally increased since 2007. It compares the value of card payments (horizontal axis) and cash in circulation (vertical axis), both as percentages of GDP, in advanced and emerging market economies.

9.1.3 The Euro Changeover
An interesting incident occurred in the run-up to the euro changeover in 2002.
It is well known that much of the cash in circulation reflects “hoarded” cash, generally held in high denominations.
Imagine yourself in 2001, with a huge pile of 500 Deutsche Mark notes because you run what we might call “an informal business.” Would you have fancied walking into a bank in early 2002 to get the whole pile changed into euros?
Hence, currency in circulation in the euro area gradually fell from €340 billion in January 2001 to €234 billion in December 2001, and then gradually recovered. Most of the cash taken out of circulation was deposited in banks.
There was a big decline and then a big increase in the average value of banknotes in circulation. (The lecture refers to an article on the ECB website.) The €500 note has been very popular with “informal” businesses.

9.2 The Money Supply and the Money Multiplier
We will now describe a simple model of how the central bank can control measures of the money supply, such as M1, by controlling the monetary base. Problems with this model are discussed in the next lecture.
Central banks do not have direct control over these aggregates. Here we describe how monetarists saw the relationship between the quantity of reserves and the M1 measure of the money supply.

9.2.1 Money Creation via loans
Let’s start by considering a very simple world where all banks are just starting up in business and do not yet have any sources of funds. Let \(r\) be the reserve requirement ratio. After an initial increase of 1 in the monetary base, the subsequent increases are \(1-r\), \((1-r)^2\), \((1-r)^3\), and so on.

9.2.2 The Money Multiplier
The money multiplier is the ratio of the money supply to the monetary base. In this simple example, it equals:
\[
m=\frac{M1}{MB}=\frac{1}{r}.
\]
The money multiplier is often misinterpreted.
In our example, the central bank starts by increasing deposits by $100, and the actions of the banking system end up increasing deposits by $1,000.
People sometimes think that individual banks can somehow take in $100 and then make an additional $900 in loans from this, creating funds out of nowhere. The lecturer argues that this would amount to lending funds they did not have, which would be fraud.
That is not what happens in this example. In each case, banks lend 90% of their deposits and retain the rest. They do not lend out amounts above those provided to them by depositors, which is their role as financial intermediaries.
When a person deposits $100 in cash in a bank, that bank can lend at most an additional $100. However, in a fractional-reserve system with a reserve requirement of 10%, $100 of reserves is consistent with $1,000 of total deposits.


9.2.3 Balance Sheet with Deposits Staying Within the Bank

Most loans are issued for the purpose of spending on particular things. Why take out a loan just to leave it sitting in the bank on deposit, since this will lose you money? The money gets spent and ends up in deposit accounts at other banks.
If, for whatever reason, the loaned money remained in the bank as deposits, a bank choosing to meet only the minimum reserve requirement (as assumed here) could use these reserves to make new loans, just as other banks did in the example.



9.2.4 Create Deposits
Notice something about the money multiplier story: Loans create deposits. Economists have been teaching this for a long time.
But people who argue that “banks are not financial intermediaries” often also say that “economists teach you that deposits create loans but it is really loans that create deposits.” The lecturer argues that this confuses different things.
At the level of an individual bank, economists usually do not teach that a loan first shows up as a deposit within the same bank. (This is the “loans creating deposits” step that, as the lecturer notes, is not usually taught in the introductory presentation, although he showed it here.)
There are good reasons for this teaching choice. Most of the money banks lend does not work this way: one needs to follow the initial step with the borrower spending the money, which most likely shows up in a different bank, just like the traditional story.
Individual banks are financial intermediaries and need deposits to issue loans.
But at the level of the banking system as a whole, loans create deposits.

title: 9  Money Supply
text:
9.3 Incorporating Currency and Excess Reserves
The previous example did not allow for the possibility that some loan proceeds would be withdrawn as currency, rather than just re-deposited in the banking system.
Now assume currency is a constant fraction \(c\) of deposits:
\[
C=cD.
\]
The previous example also assumed banks would maintain a reserve ratio of \(r\). Banks may want to hold more reserves for precautionary reasons. Assume that reserves are:
\[
R=(r+e)D,
\]
where \(e\) represents excess reserves as a fraction of deposits.
The monetary base is:
\[
MB=R+C=(r+e+c)D.
\]
The M1 money supply is:
\[
M1=D+C=(1+c)D.
\]
The money multiplier is thus:
\[
\boxed{m=\frac{M1}{MB}=\frac{1+c}{r+e+c}.}
\]
The money multiplier gets smaller as \(e\) gets bigger. It also gets smaller as \(c\) gets bigger, provided \(r+e<1\) (which the lecture assumes will be the case).

title: 9  Money Supply
section: 9.4 Friedman and Schwartz on the Great Depression
text:
9.4 Friedman and Schwartz on the Great Depression
Through careful collection of data that had not previously been available, Friedman and Schwartz’s famous 1963 study, A Monetary History of the United States, 1867–1960, showed that \(e\) and \(c\) increased during the Great Depression and that there was a sharp decline in the money multiplier.
The underlying cause was a banking crisis, which led to a lack of confidence in banks.
Depositors withdrew money from banks they viewed as perhaps not being safe, preferring to keep it as cash, and banks needed to keep large stocks of reserves in case they were hit by a bank run.
The Federal Reserve during the 1930s did not collect detailed monetary statistics and had not been aware that the money supply was sharply contracting.
Friedman and Schwartz attributed the decline in economic activity to the sharp contraction of the money supply.
The figure tracks the currency ratio \(c\) and the excess-reserves ratio \(e\) from 1929 to 1933. Both increased around the banking crises, illustrating the mechanisms described on Slide 25.
