15.1.2 The Eurosystems’s QE
The ECB did not implement QE during either the global financial crisis of 2008/09 or the Euro crisis period of 2010 to 2012. Only in 2015 did the ECB implement an “Asset Purchase Programme” (APP) in response to inflation being persistently below its 2 percent target.
The APP saw each of the central banks and the ECB buying assets. The ECB bought 8 percent of the assets and the other 92 percent were bought by national central banks in proportion to their “capital key” (an average of their share in the euro area’s population and their share in GDP).
The APP bought some privately-issued bonds but mainly bought government securities, with each national central bank only buying securities issued by their own national government.
From March 2020 to March 2022, there was a “Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme” (PEPP) with purchases of € 1.8 trillion in assets.
Like the Fed, the Eurosystem is now very gradually reducing its asset holdings, taking payment on maturing assets and not actively selling securities.

section: 15.2 Why Do Central Banks Implement QE?
text:
15.2 Why Do Central Banks Implement QE?
Central banks implement QE to reduce long-term yields in important financial markets such as the markets for government bonds and mortgage-backed securities. They hope that by lowering these key benchmark rates, interest rates on other types of borrowing will also fall.
They also hope these interventions, by lowering bond yields, will increase asset prices and this will boost spending in the economy.
Let’s discuss how central banks think QE can influence bond yields.

15.2.1 Can Central Banks Influence Other Interest Rates?
Even when short-term money-market interest rates are zero or negative, important borrowing rates, such as mortgage rates, may still be positive. What can central banks do to reduce these rates?
As discussed previously, central banks can seek to lower long-term risk-free interest rates by signalling to financial markets that they intend to keep short-term interest rates low for a long time. Most major central banks have used this approach at some point over the past decade. This is the mechanism of forward guidance.
According to the models developed earlier in the course, however, there would seem to be no other mechanism. Our framework so far has been:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{N-Year Risky Lending Rate}
&= \text{N-Year Risk-Free Rate} \\
&\quad + \text{Risk Premium}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The N-year risk-free rate is determined by expected future short-term interest rates, while the risk premium depends on default risk and the quality of collateral. In that framework, these components determine the bond yield completely. In practice, however, interest rates can also be affected through mechanisms that this formula does not capture.


15.2.2 Why There Is a Demand Curve for Bonds
The “Risk Free Rate Plus Default Risk” formula effectively assumes that all investors are the same and would only hold a bond if it delivers the interest rate set by this formula.
In practice, things are a little different. Consider, the case of a bond that was yielding 3% and then, ceteris paribus, it started to yield 2% (The bond price goes up).
Demand for this bond would fall:

All investors have to make a trade-off between risk and return but investors differ in their willingness to take risks. Some investors that may have been comfortable with the risk-return tradeoff when the bond yielded 3% but now view it as too risky at 2%.
Investors may differ in their assessment of default risk. At 3% some may have viewed the bond as better value than a risk-free bond. At 2% some of these people may change their mind and view it as worse value.

What we are describing here is a demand curve. As the price of the bond goes up (yield goes down) there is less demand for it.


15.2.3 How QE Might Work: Supply and Demand for Bonds
How are bond prices determined? If the supply of a particular bond is fixed, and demand is greater at lower prices (higher yields), its equilibrium price equates the quantity supplied and the quantity demanded.
This provides another channel through which central banks can influence yields on a particular class of bonds. When a central bank purchases a specified quantity of a specified type of bond, its purchases shift the demand curve for that bond outward. The higher demand raises the bond’s price and lowers its yield. Equivalently, one can say that the private-sector demand curve remains unchanged, but the supply of bonds available to the private sector shifts inward, raising the price.
In actual markets, bond prices are not literally set by two curves crossing. Brokers continuously match buyers and sellers, and prices change from second to second. Nevertheless, the underlying principle remains: when demand to buy bonds is strong, brokers raise prices to induce investors to sell, and the resulting increase in bond prices reduces yields.
Figure 5. A Demand Curve for Bonds.






Figure 15.5: A Demand Curve for Bonds



Figure 6. Bond Prices Set by Supply and Demand .






Figure 15.6: Bond Prices Set by Supply and Demand



Figure 7. QE Increasing Bond Prices and Reducing Yields: an outward shift in demand






Figure 15.7: QE Increasing Bond Prices and Reducing Yields





15.2.4 An Example of How Bond Buying Works
It can be hard to find “clean” examples of how QE bond buying works.
Interest rates tend to move lower after QE but this could be because QE purchases send a signal that policy rates are going to be lower, i.e. it acts as a kind of forward guidance.
Below shows a picture from a great research paper by Christoph Trebesch and Jeromin Zettelmeyer that helps to answer this question. It shows the change in yields for a set of Greek government bonds between May 7, 2010 and May 17, 2010. This is when the ECB began purchasing Greek bonds with its Securities Market Program.
The data points circled by the red line correspond to bond issues that were not purchased by the ECB, while the rest of the data points correspond to bonds that had some ECB purchases.
The striking result is that only bonds that were purchased by the ECB saw falling average yields. And the more the ECB bought, the more the yields fell.
Figure 8. How ECB Bond Purchases Affected Greek Bond Yields: changes in yields against ECB purchases as a percentage of each bond






Figure 15.8: How ECB Bond Purchases Affected Greek Bond Yields





15.2.5 Evidence on the Effects of the Fed’s QE
Given uncertainty about how it works (Ben Bernanke joked “The problem with QE is it works in practice, but it doesn’t work in theory”) were Fed officials right to believe the QE programmes have an effect?
Bernanke summarises the evidence on the impact of QE from Ihrig et al (2018) as follows:

“QE1 reduced the 10-year term premium by 34 basis points, the Maturity Extension Program reduced term premiums by an additional 28 basis points, and QE3 reduced term premiums yet more, by 31 basis points on announcement and more over time.”

In other words, about $3.5 trillion dollars worth of money created to buy long-term bonds managed to reduce long-term yields by less than one percentage point. So while QE programmes can have an impact on interest rates, it is clear that it takes very large amounts of “money printing” in the form of QE to obtain a relatively small impact on long-term rates.

title: 15  Quantitative Easing
text:
15.3 QE-Related Myths and Controversies
There are a lot of misunderstandings and myths around QE. Here, We will discuss:

QE as “Pumping money into banks to increase lending.”
QE boosting bank profits.
QE as a form of debt monetisation.
How QE has influenced recent developments for central bank profits.


15.3.1 QE and Bank Lending
Historical documents show that Ben Bernanke, the Fed chair who introduced QE, did not believe that QE would boost bank lending. The following statements from Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings illustrate these views.

“The Japanese approach, the quantitative easing approach, was focused on the liability side of the balance sheet—specifically the quantity of bank reserves, the monetary base, or however you want to put it, in the system.
The theory behind quantitative easing was that providing enormous amounts of very cheap liquidity to banks would encourage them to lend and that lending, in turn, would increase the broader measures of the money supply, which in turn would raise prices and stimulate asset prices, and so on, and that would suffice to stimulate the economy.
… I think that the verdict on quantitative easing is fairly negative. It didn’t seem to have a great deal of effect, mostly because banks would not lend out the reserves that they were holding. The one thing that it did seem to do was affect expectations of policy rates because everyone understood it would take some time to unwind the quantitative easing. Therefore, that pushed out into the future the increase in the policy rate.”

Fed Economists Joe Gagnon stated on QE at the March 2009 FOMC Meeting:

“A memo circulated to the FOMC last December reviewed the economic literature on this question and reported that a Federal Reserve purchase of $500 billion of long-term Treasury securities could plausibly reduce the 10-year Treasury yield by 20 to 100 basis points. Such a purchase would also be expected to lower long-term private yields. Generally speaking, public and private long-term debt markets are closely linked, and correlations of changes in yields across these markets have historically been very high.”

Dave Reifschneider stated:

“The top panel of your next exhibit reviews the basic channels through which buying agency MBS or long-term Treasury securities potentially influences the real economy. The primary mechanism is through a broad improvement in financial conditions. As Joe discussed, such purchases reduce yields on the targeted securities. In addition, the evidence suggests that these reductions spill over to yields on corporate bonds and other long-term instruments; if so, these interest rate movements should spark higher equity prices and a lower real exchange rate. In turn, household spending, business investment, and net exports should strengthen in response to lower borrowing costs, higher wealth, and greater international price competitiveness.”

Actually, the money multiplier slumped when the Fed introduced QE because banks did not increase their lending by much at the time. And staff briefings about QE at the time indicated the point of the policy was that it would lower long-term Treasury and mortgage rates.


15.3.2 QE and Bank Profits
Some commentators claim that QE is a programme intended to benefit banks. They may know that QE involves the Fed crediting the accounts commercial banks hold with it, but overlook the rest of the transaction.
As discussed earlier in the course when examining open market operations, banks are neither better nor worse off simply because of these operations. They acquire an additional asset in the form of reserves held at the central bank, but also acquire an additional liability in the form of a deposit owed to the person who sold the security to the central bank (as in the earlier example involving Janet).
Furthermore, for much of the period discussed in the lecture during which QE programmes operated, banks earned zero interest on their reserves. The lecturer’s conclusion is that QE was not a “secret bailout” for banks.


15.3.3 QE as Stealth Fiscal Policy
Others argue that QE is a form of debt monetisation—a hidden fiscal policy under which the government is financed by money created by the central bank. Such a description could apply if central banks directly purchased newly issued government bonds from the government.
However, the major central bank QE programmes discussed here involved purchases of securities in secondary markets. Central banks bought government-issued bonds from private-sector holders. Thus the private sector initially financed government borrowing, even though the central bank subsequently became the holder of the bonds.
QE clearly has some fiscal effects:

It lowers the interest rate on government debt, making it easier to spend more or tax less.
The interest payments on bonds owned by the central bank boost its profits and get returned to central government, lowering the net interest cost of the debt.

But conventional monetary policies also have fiscal consequences so this isn’t a new thing.


15.3.4 QE and Central Bank Profits Today
QE was introduced at a time when policy rates were zero around the world. Today, when policy rates are much higher, the combination of higher policy rates, large bond holdings by central banks and a large supply of commercial bank reserves is having negative fiscal consequences.

The bonds acquired during the QE programmes typically had low yields.
Because QE has only been very partially unwinded, there is still a very large supply of reserves.
And central banks are paying interest on reserves at their policy rate.

This means the cost of paying interest on reserves is exceeding the interest earned on the bonds acquired during QE. Central banks, which had made large profits over the previous decade, are now losing money which means they are not passing profits back to central governments anymore. In some cases, the magnitudes of this effect is large. One option to reduce this cost would be to use tiering when paying interest on reserves: Pay interest on the marginal reserves but not on all reserves. We know from the negative rate era that this works to set market rates, so why implement monetary policy in a way that has higher fiscal costs?

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.2 Phillips curve
How does economic strength translate into inflation?
An early version of this idea was the so-called Phillips curve, named after LSE economist A. W. Phillips, who published a paper on the subject in 1958. The idea behind the Phillips curve was that inflation would be high when the unemployment rate was low, and inflation would be low when unemployment was high.

The proposed mechanism starts when the economy is doing well and there is substantial demand for goods and services. Employers hire more workers, and the unemployment rate becomes low.
Workers are then in high demand and can obtain higher wage increases.
These increases in wage costs raise costs for firms, resulting in higher price inflation.

A 1960 study by MIT economists Solow and Samuelson replicated these findings for the United States and emphasised that the relationship also worked for price inflation. The Phillips curve tradeoff quickly became the basis for discussions of macroeconomic policy.

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.3 The Expectations-Augmented Phillips Curve
In a famous presidential address to the American Economics Association, Milton Friedman (1968) pointed out that it was expected real wages that affected wage bargaining.
If low unemployment gives workers a strong bargaining position, then high nominal wage inflation alone is not enough. Workers want nominal wage inflation to exceed price inflation.
Assuming that wage inflation is passed through to price inflation, this gives the expectations-augmented Phillips curve:
\[
\pi_t = \pi_t^e - \gamma(U_t-U^*)
\]
Friedman argued that if policy-makers tried to exploit an apparent Phillips curve tradeoff, the public would become accustomed to high inflation and come to expect it. Expected inflation, \(\pi_t^e\), would drift upwards, worsening the tradeoff between inflation and output.
In the long run, policy-makers cannot fool the public: \(\pi_t^e \approx \pi_t\). As a result, unemployment cannot be kept away from its natural rate, so \(U_t\approx U^*\).

Figure 16.4: Friedman’s 1977 graph on the expectations-adjusted Phillips curve

section: 16.4 The Demise of the Basic Phillips Curve
text:
16.4 The Demise of the Basic Phillips Curve
US monetary and fiscal policies in the 1960s were very expansionary. At first, the Phillips curve seemed to work: inflation rose, and unemployment fell. However, as the public became accustomed to high inflation, the Phillips curve tradeoff worsened. By the late 1960s, inflation was still rising even though unemployment had also increased.
This combination of high inflation and high unemployment, known as stagflation, became even worse in the 1970s. This was exactly what Friedman had predicted. The data no longer show any clear negative relationship between inflation and unemployment, and the original formulation of the Phillips curve is widely regarded as wrong. The 1960s are now seen as an example of what can go wrong when monetary policy pursues the wrong goals.

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.5 The Accelerationist Phillips Curve
What determines inflation expectations? Friedman argued that they are determined adaptively. For example, people might use last year’s inflation rate as a guide to what to expect this year. In that case, \(\pi_t^e = \pi_{t-1}\), and the expectations-augmented Phillips curve becomes
\[
\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} - \gamma(U_t-U^*)
\]
This equation relates the change in inflation to the gap between unemployment and its natural rate. When unemployment is below its natural rate, inflation will be increasing; when unemployment is above its natural rate, inflation will be decreasing. Because the model relates the rate of acceleration of the price level to unemployment, it is known as the accelerationist Phillips curve. This model fitted the data quite well for a long time.
Figure 7. Unemployment and annual changes in US inflation, 1955–2024. Inflation changes are measured as the change in four-quarter inflation relative to a year earlier






Figure 16.7: Scatterplot of unemployment against the change in inflation, 1955–2024



The accelerationist Phillips curve, relating changes in inflation to the unemployment rate, appears to offer a key tool to central bankers, and it is indeed useful. However, the real world is more complicated than this simple model. Two complications are particularly important:

16.5.1 Supply Shocks
Supply shocks, such as large increases or decreases in food or energy prices, can temporarily shift the inflation–unemployment tradeoff. In this case, the equation becomes
\[
\Delta\pi_t=-\gamma(U_t-U^*)+s_t
\]
Bad supply shocks are those that raise inflation even though the unemployment rate has not changed. Oil-price shocks are a good example.


16.5.2 The natural rate of unemployment
The natural rate of unemployment, \(U^*\), is not a universal constant. It probably changes over time, and central bankers must estimate it at any particular moment. For example, the natural rate in Europe rose substantially in the 1980s and 1990s. More generally, central bankers are usually uncertain about how fast the economy can grow without triggering inflationary pressures.


16.5.3 Tradeoffs Offered by the Accelerationist Phillips Curve
Over the short term, the accelerationist model describes a new tradeoff for central bankers. For example, they can choose to keep unemployment below the natural rate temporarily at the expense of increasing inflation. However, the model does not really offer an exploitable long-run tradeoff.
Even if central bankers wanted to be popular and maintain unemployment below its natural rate, the cost of ever-increasing inflation would be too high. Furthermore, if they tried to exploit this relationship, people would recognise the policy and adjust their expectations. They would probably stop setting \(\pi_t^e=\pi_{t-1}\), and the relationship would break down.
Policy-makers therefore have to accept that, over the long run, unemployment will be close to its natural rate. In this situation, they should commit to a low inflation rate. Nevertheless, the distinction between a tradeoff that can be exploited to some extent in the short run but not in the long run remains important.


16.5.4 Implications for Central Bank Institutional Design
The expectations-augmented Phillips curve suggests that the best outcome is obtained when the central bank can commit to low inflation and the public believes this commitment. This suggests several approaches to central bank institutional design.

Political independence is important because a central bank that plans for the long term, rather than worrying about economic performance during election years, is more likely to maintain its commitment to low inflation. Independence from political control can therefore reassure the public about the central bank’s credibility. Influential research by Alesina and Summers (1993) showed that more independent central banks were associated with lower inflation.
Conservative central bankers may also improve outcomes. If a central banker strongly dislikes inflation, and the public believes this, the economy can move closer to the ideal low-inflation outcome without having to raise unemployment. The government may therefore appoint a central banker who is more inflation-averse than the government itself. Paul Volcker’s appointment as Fed chair in 1979 might be an example.
Consequences for bad inflation outcomes provide another way to establish credibility. Introducing laws that impose adverse consequences on central bankers when inflation is high can help convince the public that they will adhere to a low-inflation commitment.

Figure 8. Central bank independence and average inflation across countries, as reported by Alesina and Summers (1993)






Figure 16.8: Alesina and Summers evidence on central bank independence and inflation





16.5.5 Influence of This Research
These ideas had a considerable influence on the legal structure of central banks around the world.

Political independence has increased substantially. For example, the Bank of England was made independent in 1997; previously, the Chancellor of the Exchequer had set interest rates. The ECB/Eurosystem is also highly independent of political control.
The idea of conservative central bankers has also become influential. Central bankers around the world now speak much more about the evils of inflation and the benefits of price stability. They mainly do so because they believe these claims, but there is also a marketing element: the public’s belief in a commitment to low inflation may improve the macroeconomic tradeoff available to the central bank.
consequences for bad inflation outcomes have become more common. Many central banks have legally imposed inflation targets, with penalties or formal obligations when the target is not met. For instance, the Governor of the Bank of England must write a letter to the Chancellor explaining why the inflation target was not achieved.

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.6 Discussion of Low Inflation

16.6.1 Long-Run Benefits of Low Inflation
Because central banks now believe that they cannot reliably control unemployment or economic growth over long periods, they tend to focus on what they believe they can control: inflation. In recent years, most central banks have aimed to keep inflation low and stable as their main goal.
Former Fed chair Ben Bernanke, in his speech The Benefits of Price Stability, argued that

“the mandated goals of price stability and maximum employment are almost entirely compatible.”

Low inflation can support long-run economic growth by

saving the time and energy associated with dealing with high inflation, such as regularly resetting prices or rewriting contracts.
It can facilitate long-run decision-making because consumers and businesses do not need to worry as much about uncertainty concerning the future price level.
It can also improve the price signals on which the market system relies.

However, it is difficult to argue on these grounds that there is a large welfare gain from reducing inflation from, for example, 4% to 2%.


16.6.2 Problems with a Low Inflation Target
Most central banks have adopted an inflation target of approximately 2% over the past two decades, and inflation has generally been kept in check in advanced economies since the mid-1980s.
More recently, there has been debate over whether a 2% inflation target is too low. When inflation averages 2%, relatively small shocks can bring the economy close to deflation. A higher inflation target might give central banks more room to reduce interest rates before reaching lower bounds on policy rates and having to use unconventional policies such as quantitative easing (QE).
The paper by Blanchard et al., Rethinking Macroeconomic Policy, and Ben Bernanke’s blog post The Zero Lower Bound on Interest Rates discuss the potential benefits and costs of higher inflation targets.
There have also been signs that some policy-makers are reconsidering a focus purely on inflation targeting. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand, the first pure inflation targeter in the 1990s, was given a changed mandate in March 2018 that required it also to take employment into account when making monetary policy decisions.

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.7 Inflation

16.7.1 Low Inflation Prior to 2021
Prior to 2021, inflation had been low in advanced economies for years despite many of these economies experiencing very low unemployment. Some commentators speculated that “the Phillips curve is dead,” meaning central banks no longer needed to worry about overheating economies generating higher inflation.
Several explanations were proposed.

First, the unemployment rate may have become a poor summary measure of the balance between supply and demand in the economy.
Second, in an increasingly globalised economy, the relevant supply capacity determining inflation may be global rather than national, with low inflation reflecting spare capacity in the world economy.
Third, after many years of low inflation, the public’s inflation expectations may have remained anchored around 2%.

In his 2021 paper Central Banks and Inflation: Where Do We Stand and How Did We Get Here?, Karl Whelan wrote:

“the laws of supply and demand have not been repealed. There is a strong body of empirical evidence telling us that macroeconomic policy can influence aggregate demand and there is little reason to doubt that stimulating aggregate demand sufficiently can raise inflation.” Recent experience supports this view.



16.7.2 The Phillips Curve and Recent Inflation
Much of the recent surge in inflation, particularly in the euro area, was due to supply shocks, which are not part of the basic Phillips curve relationship. However, part of the increase stemmed from the effects of fiscal and monetary stimulus on aggregate demand.
The unemployment rate probably is not a very good summary measure, if it ever was, of imbalances between supply and demand. Nevertheless, central bankers have clearly continued to use the expectations-augmented Phillips curve to frame their thinking about how to reduce inflation.
Central banks such as the Fed and the ECB raised interest rates to slow economic activity and reduce inflation. They also expressed concern that high inflation could de-anchor inflation expectations, potentially leading to a return of stagflation.
However, increases in longer-term inflation expectations measured by surveys of consumers and professional economists were relatively restrained. This suggested that the public largely expected the high inflation rates to be temporary.

title: 16  The Phillips Curve: Evidence and Implications
text:
16.8 MMT
In the years before the pandemic, the absence of inflation and the weak relationship between money supply and prices prompted some high-profile alternative approaches to monetary policy.
The school known as Modern Monetary Theory (MMT), associated most notably with Stefanie Kelton, promotes the idea that government spending should be financed by central bank money creation rather than taxes, up to the point where such financing causes inflation.
MMT advocates are correct that this is technically a possible way to run macroeconomic policy. However, this raises important questions. Would a central bank tasked with financing government spending be sufficiently independent to restrain inflation when it rises? Would governments actually adjust spending and taxes to control inflation?
Over the long run, there is a relatively simple reason why financing government spending through central bank money creation is not a magic solution. If the government wants to increase real government spending, the required resources must come from the private sector. This transfer can happen through taxes that reduce private incomes, or through higher prices that act as an inflation tax.

title: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule
text:
17.1 Real Interest Rates
We have described how central banks control short-term interest rates on interbank loans. We have also described how longer-term interest rates are affected by expectations about what will happen to short-term rates in the future. It is through this mechanism that central banks influence risk-free rates at all maturities.
Considerations about default risk and collateral then need to be factored in to understand movements in interest rates for risky private-sector lending. These private-sector interest rates have a significant effect on the economy: high interest rates negatively affect the economy by discouraging spending.
But what do we mean by a high interest rate? Is ten percent a high interest rate?
It depends on the level of inflation.
crumbs: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule

title: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule
text:
17.1.1 Real Interest Rates and Consumption
Real interest rates are calculated by subtracting the rate of inflation from the rate of interest, which is also known as the nominal interest rate. If the nominal interest rate is 10%, then if inflation is 10%, the real interest rate is zero. If inflation is 5%, the real interest rate is 5%.
Consider the decision to save for tomorrow or spend today. The argument for saving is that it can allow you to consume more tomorrow. If the real interest rate is negative, this means you will be able to purchase less tomorrow with the money that you set aside. For instance, if the interest rate is 5% but inflation is 10%, then you receive 5% in interest but your savings have eroded in value by more than that.
Thus, low real interest rates discourage saving and high real interest rates encourage it.


17.1.2 Real Interest Rates and Business Investment
Consider a firm that is thinking about buying capital equipment and suppose the interest rate is 10%.

If the firm is borrowing the money, it needs to consider whether the investment will generate enough new profit income to justify paying back both the amount borrowed (the principal) and the interest.
If the firm has spare money available, it needs to consider whether it would be better off putting the money in the bank at the prevailing interest rate rather than buying the machine.

Either way, the higher the interest rate, the less likely the firm is to buy the equipment. Again, inflation matters when thinking about whether an interest rate is considered high. If inflation is 10%, the firm can expect that its profits will be increasing by that much and a 10% interest rate will not seem so high. But if prices are falling, then a 10% interest rate on borrowings will seem very high.
Low real interest rates encourage business investment and high real interest rates discourage it.
crumbs: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule

title: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule
text:
17.2 The Taylor Rule
We have covered material that helps explain roughly how modern central banks should behave, including policies to influence interest rates and the implications of the expectations-augmented Phillips curve. But this does not address the basic operational question: How should a central bank decide what is the right interest rate to set at any point in time?
Here we discuss a famous monetary policy “rule,” first discussed in a 1993 paper by Stanford economist John Taylor. Much of the discussion of monetary policy today uses the so-called Taylor rule as a benchmark for how policy should be conducted. We will describe the rule and how it would be implemented, discuss how well it explains actual policy, and consider its relevance to current US monetary policy.

17.2.1 The Taylor Rule and Real Interest Rates
Taylor’s rule says that the Federal Reserve should set the federal funds rate according to the following formula:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Federal Funds Rate} = {}& \text{Inflation Rate} \\
& + 0.5(\text{Inflation Rate} - 2\%) \\
& + 0.5(\text{Gap Between Real GDP and Its Trend}) \\
& + 2\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, if the inflation rate were 4% and the gap between real GDP and its trend level (known as the output gap) were minus 1%, the Taylor rule would recommend setting the federal funds rate equal to 6.5%, because
\[
4 + 0.5(4-2) + 0.5(-1) + 2 = 6.5.
\]
The “Inflation Rate minus 2%” term in the rule relies on the assumption that 2% is the Fed’s target rate of inflation. The idea of reacting to real GDP differing from its trend comes from the Phillips curve: above-trend values of GDP may signal an increase in inflation, while below-trend values may signal a fall in inflation.
Note that when inflation goes up, the rule says that the federal funds rate should go up by more. Specifically, a one-percentage-point increase in inflation should be matched by a 1.5-percentage-point increase in the federal funds rate.
This means there is an increase in the real interest rate when inflation rises. The real interest rate is the actual, or nominal, interest rate set by the Fed minus inflation.
Taylor had a very specific recommendation for how the Fed should respond to inflation: raise the federal funds rate by 1.5 percentage points for every one-percentage-point increase in inflation. But the general idea that policy rates should change by more than the change in inflation is now known as the Taylor principle.






Tip



Let’s See If You Understand the Taylor Principle


A central bank responds to inflation rising from 2 percent to 3 percent by increasing the policy interest rate from 1 percent to 2.5 percent. Does this action conform to the Taylor principle?
Inflation rose from 2% to 3%, so it increased by one percentage point. The policy interest rate rose from 1% to 2.5%, so it increased by 1.5 percentage points. The policy interest rate rose by more than the inflation rate, so yes, this action satisfies the Taylor principle.


17.2.2 The Fed and the Taylor Principle
Many studies of the so-called Great Inflation of the 1970s argue that the Fed did not obey the Taylor principle during that decade. They allowed real interest rates to fall when inflation rose, which further fueled inflation. This lack of responsiveness of policy to inflation helps explain why inflation became so high during the 1970s.
Historical evidence, such as Allan Meltzer’s History of the Federal Reserve, points out that there was little discussion at the Fed of the concept of real interest rates during the 1970s until Paul Volcker became chair. Estimates of the responsiveness of the federal funds rate to inflation since 1979 are significantly higher than in the prior period.
Other researchers have pointed to the uncertainty in estimates of the output gap at the time as a complicating factor. The Fed continually mistook what was a permanent slowdown in average growth rates for a transitory one.
This shows one drawback of the Taylor rule: it requires an estimate of the gap between output and its “non-inflationary” potential level. In practice, obtaining estimates of this gap is fraught with difficulties.


17.2.3 The Long-Run Real Interest Rate
Recall the original Taylor rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Federal Funds Rate} = {}& \text{Inflation Rate} \\
& + 0.5(\text{Inflation Rate} - 2\%) \\
& + 0.5(\text{Output Gap}) + 2\%.
\end{aligned}
\]
The number 2% features twice in Taylor’s rule, representing two different concepts. As well as the “Inflation Rate minus 2%” term, the rule contains the “+2%” element at the end.
How should this second term be interpreted? Suppose the gap between GDP and its trend were zero and inflation equaled the Fed’s target of 2%. Then the federal funds rate would equal 4% and the real interest rate would be 2%.
Since the rule was designed to deliver average inflation of zero and since GDP should on average equal its trend, this meant Taylor was recommending an average long-run real interest rate of 2%.

section: 17.3 An Updated Implementation of the Taylor Rule
text:
17.3 An Updated Implementation of the Taylor Rule
Since Taylor’s paper, there has been a great deal of additional research on monetary policy rules. In May 2009, Glenn Rudebusch of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco published a paper with a “Taylor rule” constructed to match the average behavior of the Fed over the period 1988 to 2008.
Rudebusch used core consumer prices to measure inflation and an unemployment gap instead of an output gap. This unemployment gap was constructed as the difference between the unemployment rate and the Congressional Budget Office’s (CBO) estimate of the so-called natural rate of unemployment.
Estimating the relationship with data from 1988 to 2008 gives the following rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Federal Funds Rate} = {}& 0.75 + 1.75(\text{Core Inflation}) \\
& - 1.71(\text{Unemployment Gap}).
\end{aligned}
\]
This rule implied that there should have been highly negative federal funds rates during the global financial crisis and again during the COVID pandemic. The lecturer updated this rule using monthly data through October 2023.

17.3.1 How Constraining Was the Zero Bound?
The Fed has never cut the federal funds rate below zero. Our update of Rudebusch’s graph suggests that this stopped the Fed from implementing rates consistent with the Taylor rule during and after the global financial crisis, and also during the pandemic. After the financial crisis, the federal funds rate suggested by the rule remained negative until early 2014. During the global pandemic, the rule again suggested that the funds rate should have been slashed to minus 12%.
This makes it look as though the zero bound seriously constrained the Fed. But looks can be deceiving. A 2018 paper by Eric Swanson pointed out that even when the Fed kept its policy rate at zero, it was able to move long-term rates—which matter more for the economy—through quantitative easing and forward guidance. Swanson suggested that the responsiveness of long-term interest rates to economic news did not change much during the period when the federal funds rate was zero. This suggests that the Fed was still able to convince markets it had the tools to influence the economy.

title: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule
section: 17.4 The Fed and the Taylor Rule Prior to 2020
text:
17.4 The Fed and the Taylor Rule Prior to 2020
In the years prior to the pandemic, the Fed had clearly departed from following the Taylor rule. The Taylor rule’s recommended policy rate turned positive in late 2013, but the Fed did not raise rates above zero until 2016. It then started cutting rates in 2019, when the rule suggested keeping them stable at a higher level.
We will focus on two reasons why the Fed departed from the Taylor rule: lower long-run real interest rates and less concern about inflation.

17.4.1 Lower Long-Term Average Real Rates
Recall Rudebusch’s rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Federal Funds Rate} = {}& 0.75 + 1.75(\text{Core Inflation}) \\
& - 1.71(\text{Unemployment Gap}).
\end{aligned}
\]
From this, we can calculate that the long-run average real interest rate consistent with 2% inflation is 2.25%, because
\[
2.25 = 0.75 + 1.75\times 2 - 2.
\]
However, Fed officials do not believe the average real interest rate in the future will be this high. FOMC members provide forecasts for macroeconomic variables such as inflation and for the federal funds rate, including a “longer-run” forecast.
In January 2012, the FOMC’s median estimate of the long-run real federal funds rate was 2.25%. In recent years, this estimate has been 0.5%. This implies that they think interest rates should be 1.75 percentage points lower on average now than in the past.
Why? Macroeconomists now largely agree that equilibrium real interest rates are lower than they used to be, with various explanations offered, including demographics and weak productivity growth.


17.4.2 Less Concern About Inflation
The idea of raising interest rates when unemployment is low, or the output gap is positive, rests on the Phillips curve: the idea that low unemployment signals higher future inflation.
However, in the years prior to the pandemic, inflation was consistently low in advanced economies despite many of them experiencing low unemployment for extended periods of time.
Many speculated that “the Phillips curve is dead,” so central banks no longer needed to worry about economies overheating and generating higher inflation. By 2020, the Fed had made clear that it had decided to keep interest rates low as long as inflation remained contained and to stop worrying about the potential inflationary implications of low unemployment.
In a reformulation of its monetary policy, the Fed said that it would worry less about strong labor market conditions than it had previously. In August 2020, Fed Chair Powell said that under the new approach to monetary policy,

“employment can run at or above real-time estimates of its maximum level without causing concern, unless accompanied by signs of unwanted increases in inflation.”

title: 17  Real Interest Rates and the Taylor Rule
text:
17.5 High Inflation and Monetary Tightening
After many years of low inflation, the world suddenly had plenty of “unwanted inflation” in 2021. Inflation in all advanced economies increased in 2021 and exceeded 10% in some countries in 2022. Inflation was driven both by strong aggregate demand, partly due to expansionary policies during the pandemic, and by large increases in food and energy prices due to the war in Ukraine.
Central banks responded by raising policy interest rates, but by much less than the Taylor rule would recommend. Why did they not increase rates by more?

First, central banks anticipated that the effect of war-related supply shocks on inflation would quickly ease.
Second, they were concerned that a global recession might be approaching, implying falling inflation.
Third, the real interest rate that matters for the economy is probably not the short-term policy rate minus the current backward-looking measure of inflation. Longer-term real rates—defined as long-term rates minus expected inflation—did increase.

title: 18  Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro
text:
18.1 Exchange Rates and Interest Rates
We have talked a lot about interest rates but have not yet focused on another important aspect of monetary policy: exchange rates. To understand why exchange rates matter, consider the euro–pound exchange rate, defined as €1 = £\(X\).
crumbs: Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro
18  Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro

title: 18  Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro
text:
18.1.1 Exchange Rates and Economic Growth
Suppose \(X\) increases, so that the euro becomes worth more pounds. What happens to exports and imports?

For exports, each pound of sterling revenue earned by an Irish firm now translates into fewer euros unless the firm increases the price charged to UK customers. Exporting therefore becomes less profitable and total exports decline. If the firm instead attempts to maintain its profits by raising its UK price, demand for its products falls, so exports still decline.
For imports, UK firms receive more euro revenue from selling to Ireland at unchanged prices and may therefore export more to Ireland. Alternatively, they may lower their euro-denominated prices in Ireland, gaining market share while maintaining the same sterling revenue per unit. In either case, Ireland’s imports increase.

Although an increase in the value of the euro may sound desirable for Ireland, it tends to reduce exports, increase imports and consequently reduce Irish GDP. In contrast, a currency depreciation boosts exports and has a positive effect on economic growth. This is why depreciation is often welcomed during a recession and why losing the ability to depreciate is commonly identified as a disadvantage of fixed exchange rate regimes.
Depreciation nevertheless has costs.

Inflation may increase because imported goods become more expensive. This is one reason central bankers often express a preference for a strong currency; the inflationary effect is particularly important in small open economies that import heavily.
Furthermore, the boost to growth is temporary. Over time, higher import prices may feed into higher wages, gradually eroding the initial improvement in international competitiveness.



18.1.2 Exchange Rates and Bond Yields
Suppose capital can flow freely between the United States and the euro area, and investors can purchase risk-free one-period bonds in either market. Let \(i_t^E\) denote the European bond interest rate and \(i_t^{US}\) the US bond interest rate. Investing $1 in a US bond at time \(t\) therefore delivers \(1+i_t^{US}\) dollars at time \(t+1\). For example, when the US interest rate is 4%, \(i_t^{US}=0.04\), and $1 invested now pays $1.04 next period.
Define \(e_t\) as the number of US dollars obtainable for one euro. A risk-neutral US investor has 2 options:

keep her money invested in US bonds and receive \(1+i_t^{US}\) dollars next period.
Alternatively, she can exchange her dollars for euros, purchase a European bond, and convert its proceeds back into dollars at the exchange rate prevailing next period. The latter strategy yields

\[
(1+i_t^E)\frac{e_{t+1}}{e_t}
\]
dollars per dollar initially invested.
Which investment will she choose?


18.1.3 Uncovered Interest Parity
Risk-neutral investors care only about expected returns. They prefer euro-denominated bonds when
\[
(1+i_t^E)\frac{E_t e_{t+1}}{e_t}>1+i_t^{US},
\]
where \(E_t e_{t+1}\) denotes the exchange rate for next period expected at time \(t\). They prefer dollar-denominated bonds when
\[
(1+i_t^E)\frac{E_t e_{t+1}}{e_t}<1+i_t^{US}.
\]
The theory of uncovered interest parity (UIP) states that bond yields adjust until investors are indifferent between holding domestic and foreign bonds. As in the expectations theory of long-term interest rates, the idea is based on arbitrage in financial markets: financial prices should adjust so that investors cannot systematically outperform others through an obvious investment strategy. Thus UIP predicts
\[
\boxed{(1+i_t^E)\frac{E_t e_{t+1}}{e_t}=1+i_t^{US}.}
\]


18.1.4 Uncovered Interest Parity and Expected Exchange Rates
The UIP condition implies that if European interest rates are lower than US interest rates, the euro must be expected to appreciate against the dollar. Rearranging gives
\[
\frac{E_t e_{t+1}}{e_t}=\frac{1+i_t^{US}}{1+i_t^E}.
\]
For relatively small interest rates, the right-hand side can be approximated by
\[
\boxed{\frac{E_t e_{t+1}}{e_t}\approx 1+i_t^{US}-i_t^E.}
\]
Consequently, if US interest rates are one percentage point above euro-area rates, the dollar is expected to decline in value by approximately 1%, or equivalently the euro is expected to appreciate by approximately 1%.


18.1.5 The Trilemma of International Finance
The lecture argues that UIP holds reasonably well in practice and implies that a country cannot simultaneously maintain

free capital mobility,
a fixed exchange rate
independent monetary policy.

This is known as the trilemma of international finance: any two of these objectives can be achieved, but not all three.

If a country allows free capital mobility while fixing its exchange rate, then \(E_t e_{t+1}=e_t\), and its interest rates must equal those in the economy to which it has pegged its currency, as illustrated by Ireland’s experience.
If a country instead allows capital to move freely while choosing its own monetary policy, so that interest rates differ across countries, its exchange rate must be free to fluctuate, as in the United Kingdom.
Finally, a country can maintain both an independent monetary policy and a fixed exchange rate only if it intervenes in capital markets to prevent investors from exploiting international arbitrage opportunities, as illustrated in the lecture by China.

For further discussion, the lecture refers to the paper by Obstfeld, Shambaugh and Taylor.

title: 18  Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro
text:
18.2 Exchange Rate Pegs
An exchange rate peg is an arrangement in which one country promises to exchange its currency at a fixed value relative to another currency. Such policies are common, particularly among small countries that peg their currency to an anchor currency, most often the US dollar.
In practice, maintaining a peg requires a sufficient supply of the asset for which the authorities have promised to exchange their currency.
Under the gold standard, before and after the First World War, currencies were pegged to gold. A country running a trade deficit would lose gold because foreigners receiving its currency in payment for exports could demand gold in exchange. A country that depleted its gold reserves might eventually be unable to maintain the promised exchange rate.
After the Second World War, the Bretton Woods system used US dollars as the principal reserve asset backing exchange rate pegs. The same logic applied: persistent trade deficits could cause a country’s holdings of US dollars or other foreign currencies to run out. One response to this situation was to abandon the existing parity and devalue the domestic currency. Devaluation could restore export competitiveness and potentially turn trade deficits into surpluses.

18.2.1 Exchange Rate Pegs and Speculation
Exchange rate pegs are often unstable because macroeconomic conditions change over time. An exchange rate that once produced an approximate balance between imports and exports may cease to be sustainable.
Pegs also create opportunities for speculation. Suppose the United Kingdom is pegging sterling to the dollar while running a persistent trade deficit. Investors may anticipate that sterling will eventually be devalued. They can withdraw sterling, convert it to dollars, and then exchange the dollars back into sterling after the devaluation. If they borrowed sterling to make the trade, they can repay the original sterling loan and retain a profit.
These incentives can create self-fulfilling exchange rate crises. Investors expecting devaluation withdraw funds, depleting central bank foreign exchange reserves and potentially forcing the very devaluation they anticipated. The pressure is asymmetric: countries running large trade surpluses at a pegged exchange rate can simply accumulate foreign currency reserves without being compelled to revalue their currencies upward.


18.2.2 Bretton Woods and the IMF
Capital did not move freely during the Bretton Woods era. The system was designed to support stable exchange rates while allowing countries to retain independent macroeconomic policies. From 1958 onward, however, current account convertibility（经常账户可兑换）permitted foreign exchange transactions undertaken to purchase goods. This compromise was intended to facilitate international trade while reducing the risk of self-fulfilling currency crises.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) could provide loans to countries whose trade deficits had depleted their holdings of gold or dollars, helping them maintain their fixed exchange rates. If temporary financial assistance could not solve the problem, countries could apply to the IMF for permission to devalue. The IMF would assess whether the trade deficit was sustainable and whether the peg should be maintained or adjusted downward. In practice, the arrangement did not always function as intended: large countries sometimes notified the IMF of a devaluation rather than seeking its prior approval.


18.2.3 European Monetary Arrangements From the 1970s
The Bretton Woods system collapsed in the early 1970s. From March 1973, major currencies began to float freely, with their prices determined in financial markets. Restrictions on international capital movements were also gradually relaxed in the following decades.
European countries nevertheless continued to value exchange rate stability and the resulting support for trade within the EU. In 1979 the EU introduced the European Monetary System (EMS), effectively a European counterpart to Bretton Woods. The German Deutsche Mark replaced the US dollar as the principal anchor currency, meaning that German monetary conditions strongly influenced the rest of the system. EMS currencies could fluctuate, but only within relatively narrow exchange rate bands.
The EMS experienced considerable instability and many devaluations between 1979 and 1987. Despite this, the system survived, partly because substantial capital controls constrained speculative attacks.

18.2.4 The “Hard EMS” Years: 1987–92
After numerous exchange rate realignments, EMS members took steps to make the system less unstable. The Basle–Nyborg agreement of 1987 provided for more active central bank intervention in foreign exchange markets to keep exchange rates close to target, better credit facilities for deficit countries, and stronger coordination of macroeconomic policies to discourage large trade deficits or surpluses.
Initially, these changes appeared successful. There were no currency realignments for five years, and the United Kingdom joined the EMS in 1990, expanding the area of planned exchange rate stability in Europe. Many observers came to believe that Europe would rapidly advance toward full Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) without further exchange rate realignments. The Delors Report of 1989 launched the plan for EMU, and the Maastricht Treaty, agreed in February 1992, formalised this intention.


18.2.5 Doubts Grow About EMU
Three developments ended the period of EMS stability.

The first was German reunification, which generated substantial public spending in Germany and a consumer boom in Eastern Europe. Germany required tighter monetary policy than other EMS members, and in summer 1992 financial markets began to anticipate that other countries would need to devalue their currencies.
The second was growing doubt about EMU. On 2 June 1992, Danish voters rejected the Maastricht Treaty in a referendum, leading investors to question whether sufficient political support existed for monetary union to proceed.
The third was the freer movement of capital. The Single European Act, which provided the foundation for the single market, required most capital controls to be removed by July 1990. International capital flows then became large enough to force exchange rate realignments, with daily foreign exchange transactions exceeding the total foreign exchange reserves held by central banks.

18.2.6 Hard EMS Falls Apart and the Road to EMU
After the Danish referendum in June 1992, investors increasingly expected currencies to be realigned through devaluations against the Deutsche Mark. The currencies of countries with wider allowable exchange rate bands—notably the UK, Spain and Italy—began to fall.
Sterling came under particularly severe pressure by September 1992, and comments by the Bundesbank President that devaluations could not be ruled out increased this pressure. The United Kingdom raised interest rates to 15% to attract capital inflows and spent $20 billion in foreign exchange reserves, approximately half of its holdings, in an unsuccessful effort to support the pound.
On 16 September 1992, remembered as Black Wednesday, the UK withdrew from the EMS and never rejoined the effort to establish monetary union. Italy withdrew on the same day. Other member countries subsequently devalued, including Ireland by 10% in January 1993. By summer 1993 the “hard EMS” had ended and exchange rates were permitted to move within much wider bands.
The crisis persuaded most EU governments that pegged exchange rates were difficult to reconcile with free capital mobility, and that full monetary union offered a better route to lasting exchange rate stability.

title: 18  Exchange Rate Regimes and the Euro
text:
18.3 Deciding to Join the Euro

18.3.1 When To Share a Currency?
When choosing whether to maintain a national currency that floats against other currencies, governments need to consider the structure of their economies. Small countries that export a large share of GDP place considerable value on stable exchange rates, especially if most exports go to one economic area. For such economies, a fixed exchange rate with the main trading partner may be desirable, and adopting the trading partner’s currency may be an even stronger option. Such small currencies are often considered too small to constitute optimal currency areas on their own.
For larger and less open countries, international trade may be less important and exchange rate stability may be less valuable. Such countries may also have economic cycles that differ from those of their trading partners and may find a shared monetary policy inappropriate. They may therefore prefer to retain their own currency and independent monetary policy.


18.3.2 Arguments for a Common European Currency
Many European countries wanted stable exchange rates against the German Deutsche Mark. Within the EMS, they had generally needed to follow German monetary policy without having a voice in German monetary decisions. A common currency would give all participating countries a say in the conduct of monetary policy.
A common currency was also expected to eliminate devaluation risk, which had increased borrowing costs for governments, firms and households in many EMS members. The experience of recurrent self-fulfilling speculative crises under fixed exchange rate arrangements strengthened the argument for full monetary union rather than a system of nominally fixed exchange rates subject to repeated crises.
Countries such as Italy, with historically weak inflation performance, hoped to gain from the credibility of Germany’s Bundesbank by participating in a new, more credible common currency. A common currency was also expected to reinforce the microeconomic benefits of the European single market, while its political significance lay in deepening European integration beyond monetary arrangements.


18.3.3 Complications for the Euro as a Common Currency
A common European currency faces several difficulties.

First, the size and economic asymmetries of the euro area mean that member countries can be at very different stages of the business cycle. A monetary policy suited to Germany, for example, may be inappropriate for Ireland or Spain.
Second, there is a lack of fiscal integration. Within a common currency area, regions experiencing economic weakness can benefit from lower tax payments and additional transfers, which helps offset their inability to run an independent regional monetary policy. This kind of fiscal insurance is less extensive in the euro area.
Third, labour mobility between EU countries is relatively limited. As a result, unemployment in a badly affected member state is less likely to be reduced by migration to stronger regions than would be the case between US states.
Fourth, the euro area lacks a fully centralised banking backstop. In the US, deposit insurance and the resolution of insolvent banks are organised centrally. The euro area has a common bank supervisor, but the lecture notes that deposit insurance and bank resolution are still likely to remain largely national responsibilities.

Figure 5. Consumer price inflation in Italy and Germany, illustrating historical differences in inflation performance. Source: FRED/OECD as reproduced in the lecture.






Figure 18.5: Inflation in Italy and Germany





18.3.4 Currency Choice for Ireland
All EU member states must allow free capital mobility as a requirement of the Single Market. Therefore, they face a choice between accepting a flexible exchange rate and relinquishing their own monetary policy independence. For Ireland, joining the euro was a complex decision, and the overall consequences of membership have been mixed.
As a small open economy, Ireland could be considered too small to form an optimal currency area by itself. However, Ireland did not have one dominant trading-partner currency: it traded extensively with the euro area, the United Kingdom and the United States. There was therefore no unambiguous choice of foreign currency against which to peg the Irish currency, and retaining a floating exchange rate might have made sense.
On the other hand, a floating currency exposes investors to possible future devaluation, and they may demand a risk premium for holding that country’s debt. Euro membership eliminated this particular devaluation risk and contributed to lower Irish interest rates. Those lower interest rates boosted economic growth. Yet during a period of exceptionally strong growth, this stimulus also undermined macroeconomic stability by helping to fuel the housing bubble and the subsequent banking crash.

title: 19  The Euro Crisis
text:
19.1.1 The Build Up to the Crisis: Sovereign Debt
With the adoption of the euro in 1999, financial markets should perhaps have seen that with no option to inflate debt away or to use financial repression, high public debt could translate into possible sovereign defaults.
However, with no advanced country sovereign defaults in living memory, markets celebrated the elimination of devaluation and inflation risk and began to price all Eurozone sovereign debt very similarly.
Public debt levels—which had previously had a big influence—now had almost no impact on government borrowing rates.
Even the signs in the early years that the EU’s fiscal rules were not being adhered to had no impact.
However, it would not be correct to say governments accumulated debt irresponsibly during this period. Debt-GDP ratios generally fell during this period.
Low sovereign debt yields fuelled self-fulfilling expectations of low default risk. While debt levels did not fall much, the cost of servicing it did e.g. Debt interest share of Italian GDP fell from 14% in 1993 to 5% in 2004, so a much smaller primary surplus was needed to stabilise the debt.
10-year sovereign bond yields of selected countries






Figure 19.3: 10-year sovereign bond yields of selected countries





19.1.2 The Build Up to the Crisis: Banks
With most of Europe now using a single currency, an integrated European financial market emerged which channelled a lot of money from Europe’s rich high-saving core (Germany, Netherlands, Austria) to its poorer lower-saving periphery (Greece, Ireland, Spain, Portugal).
With the risk of devaluation apparently gone, investors in the core countries viewed providing money to banks in peripheral countries as a much safer investment than they were prior to the euro.
Bank credit in the periphery increased through three channels.

Foreign Deposits in these banks increased substantially, particularly large corporate depositors.
Bond Funding rose as banks in countries like Ireland and Spain found it easier than before to borrow on the international bond market.
Foreign Banks Subsidiaries: Foreign banks were more likely to opene their own subsidiaries in these countries once there was no more currency mis-match.

Unfortunately, once the banks in the periphery got into trouble, the foreign deposits and bond market funding disappeared and foreign banks started shutting their subsidiaries.


19.1.3 The Build Up to the Crisis: Private Sector Debt
With money pouring into banks in the periphery and sovereign interest rates at all-time low levels, the private sector saw credit available in quantities and at costs never seen before.
This was a big asymmetric shock in the Euro Area. The change in borrowing costs had a profound effect in countries like Spain and Ireland while core states such as Germany saw no change.
Firms and households could now borrow at much lower rates and they (and their banks) believed that they could handle much larger stocks of debt.
These developments boosted domestic demand in many countries leading to a loss of competitiveness and higher current account deficits.
In countries like Ireland and Spain in particular, the huge increases in debt fueled house price bubbles and construction booms.
When the global financial crisis came, many peripheral economies were left with high levels of private sector debt and highly exposed weak banking sectors.

19.1.4 2007: A Sudden Stop
The global financial crisis that began in 2007 brought a sudden end to many of the trends that had allowed the build-up of debt in the periphery.

Re-Appearance of Sovereign Risk Premia: After a long period in which financial markets ignored sovereign default risk, global financial disruptions beginning in 2007 saw sovereign debt risk premia re-emerge with much of this increase being passed through to private sector rates.
Increases in Private Risk Premia: The Lehman Brothers default of September 2008 led to a re-pricing of financial sector risk. In particular, financial markets began focusing on the build-up of debt that occurred in peripheral Euro Area economies.
Financial Sector Deleveraging: The global crisis brought home to investors and regulators the problems associated with over-sized and over-leveraged financial institutions. As banks executed deleveraging programmes, there was a significant decline in private sector lending to peripheral economies.
Reversal of Financial Integration: With major banks in core countries having received significant assistance from governments, banks chose to deleverage via withdrawing from lending to peripheral economies rather than cut back lending in their own countries.

section: 19.2 The Failed Recovery and the Euro in Crisis
text:
19.2 The Failed Recovery and the Euro in Crisis

19.2.1 The Policy Response and Recovery
The global financial crisis hit all advanced economies hard and was the most severe seen since the Great Depression.
The crisis provoked a wide-ranging policy response from governments over 2008-09.

Fiscal Policy: Fiscal stimulus packages were introduced in many countries (though not so much in the Euro Area).
Monetary Policy: Policy rates were cut to zero (or close to it) and QE programmes started.
Liquidity Provision: Central banks played their roles as lender of last resort to the banking system, providing liquidity to replace investors who moved money out of weak banks.
Bank Supports and Restructuring: Governments provided supports to banks in the form of funding guarantees, asset insurance and funds for recapitalisation and initiated restructuring plans for failing banks.

Thanks to these measures, financial stability was restored and the global economy, including the Euro Area, began to recover during 2009 and this continued into 2010.


19.2.2 The Failed Recovery
The Euro Area recovery sputtered out in 2010 and fell back into a recession. After a small decline, the unemployment rate rose again until 2013.Three factors contributed to derailing the recovery:

fiscal austerity,
a credit crunch, and
concerns about sovereign default and euro exits.

These factors interacted with each other, particularly in the countries that had previously seen large increases in private debt.
By 2012, there was a full scale crisis in the euro area with banking crises and sovereign debt crises affecting many member states.


19.2.3 Fiscal Austerity
When the crisis hit economies hard in the 2008, some countries were in the euro area were in a position to do some fiscal stimulus to partially protect their economies from the shock.
But many were not. Some already had high debt levels. For others (e.g. Ireland) it was clear from the start that the scale of the collapse of the economy was such that the government deficit was going to explode as tax revenues collapsed so stimulus was not an option.
By 2010, there was fiscal contraction across the euro area. The hard-hit peripheral economies were still enforcing fiscal austerity while other countries removed the stimulus they had provided and moved to consolidation mode.
This meant that fiscal policy had a negative impetus on the euro area economy from 2010 to 2014.
While reckless fiscal policy did not play a big role in causing the crisis, the narrative that it did was highly influential in Germany and other core countries. An enhanced “fiscal compact” was passed but there is little evidence that following its rules would have prevented the crisis e.g. both Ireland and Spain would have been compliant.
Fiscal consolidation in the Euro Area (Source: European Fiscal Board (2021))






Figure 19.7: Fiscal consolidation in the Euro Area (Source: European Fiscal Board (2021))





19.2.4 The Credit Crunch
The global financial crisis and the ongoing economic slump meant that European banks suffered significant losses that reduced their capital.
Capital adequacy requirements are expressed as a percentage of risk-weighted assets. Banks that need to adjust their capital ratios to meet these requirements can either (a) Raise capital or (b) Reduce risk-weighted assets.
In the US, the government investment in the banks meant there was a large and quick recapitalisation of the banking system.
In the Euro Area, fiscal problems meant governments were less keen to commit public money to recapitalise banks.
This meant less capital raising than in the US and more focus on reducing risk-weighted assets, both by shrinking balance sheets and by reducing risk weights by cutting back on loans to households and businesses.

Loans to households which had risen rapidly prior to 2008 stalled after the Lehman’s bankruptcy, rose a bit during 2010 and then declined during the euro crisis years.
Loans to businesses fell in 2008, stabilised and then fell again during the euro crisis.

section: 19.3 The ECB’s Role in Resolving the Crisis: Providing Liquidity
text:
19.3 The ECB’s Role in Resolving the Crisis: Providing Liquidity

19.3.1 A Multi-Year Multi-Country Banking Crisis
The GFC of 2008/09 was a global event for all banking sectors. But Europe’s bank stresses continued for a lot longer than in other parts of the world.
Property prices continued to fall, leading to big losses for banks on mortgages and commercial property lending (the latter being the big issue in Ireland).
Depositors and investors lost faith in banks in Ireland, Spain, Greece, Portugal and Italy and continued pulling their funding and placing them in banks in countries considered safer, like Germany.
This crisis had a liquidity element (the deposit withdrawals were a slow form of bank run) and also a solvency element (many banks need to be recapitalised or shut).
We will discuss the ECB’s role in this process.


19.3.2 The ECB’s Response to the Banking Crisis
The banking crisis of 2008 was the first element of the overall euro crisis.
As discussed above, a lot of the funding that had been provided to banks in countries like Greece, Spain, Portugal and Ireland began to move back to “core” European countries.
Without support from the Eurosystem, banks in these countries would have had to default on the bonds they had issued and also perhaps be unable to honour requests for deposit withdrawals.
The ECB’s move to providing fixed-price full allotment funding and to provide longer-term funding for banks were crucial in containing the crisis.
The chart shows the large increase in ECB funding in response to the crisis and how longer-term funding replaced the short-term weekly funding previously provided.
ECB refinancing operations, long-term (orange) and main (blue)






Figure 19.10: ECB refinancing operations, long-term (orange) and main (blue)



The ECB did a good job in coping with the initial phase of the liquidity crisis. But questions can be raised about some of its later actions.


19.3.3 Recap on the Eurosystem’s Rules on Loans to Banks
The Eurosystem has a relatively clear set of rules on lending to banks:

Loans must be collateralised. There is a publicly available list of eligible collateral with “haircuts” for each asset. There are over €13 trillion of marketable assets acceptable as collateral.
Losses on regular Eurosystem loans are shared among Eurosystem central banks.

But there are some important nuances.

The composition of the eligible collateral list can change, for instance if the ECB views the credit quality of an asset as declining.
The risk control framework can be used to select individual assets or institutions as not being eligible for regular credit from ECB.

Banks can also received loans through Emergency Liquidity Assistance (ELA) ECB says

“ELA aims to provide central bank money to solvent financial institutions that are facing temporary liquidity problems, outside of normal Eurosystem monetary policy operations.”

Responsibility for ELA (and the risk involved) lies with the issuing NCB.


19.3.4 The ECB and ELA
When a bank has run out of eligible collateral for regular Eurosystem loans, it can apply for ELA. This decision occurs at a national central bank level and the NCB takes on the balance sheet risk.
But the ECB still plays a role. An example of the ECB’s description of its role (from October 2014):

The ECB neither provides nor approves emergency liquidity assistance. It is the national central bank … that provides ELA to an institution that it judges to be solvent at its own risks and under its own terms and conditions. The ECB can object on monetary policy grounds; in order to do so at least two thirds of the Governing Council must see the provision of emergency liquidity as interfering with the tasks and objectives of Euro Area monetary policy.

You could argue that the ECB’s is saying here that it doesn’t provide or approve ELA but also that it sort of does.
Procedures underlying ELA used to be secret but an “ELA agreement” was published in 2013 and updated in 2017.


19.3.5 Some Examples of ELA
Three cases of ELA provision are

Ireland (2009–2010),
Cyprus (2011–2013), and
Greece (2014–2015).


19.3.5.1 Ireland: 2009-2010

September 2008: Anglo Irish Bank runs out of eligible collateral. No ELA is provided but the Irish government provides a near-blanket guarantee.
March 2009: €11.5 billion in ELA given to Anglo, which turns out to be highly insolvent in the absence of government-provided equity investment.
2010: ELA provided to other Irish banks. Total rises to over €40 billion.
November 2010: Ireland opens negotiations to begin an EU-IMF programme. During negotiations, ECB President Trichet sends a letter to the Minister for Finance insisting Ireland enter an EU-IMF programme requiring fiscal and structural reforms as a condition for continued authorisation of ELA. The programme is agreed on November 28.
2011 onwards: ELA rises to almost €70 billion in early 2011 but begins to fall as the banking sector stabilises. Ireland successfully exits the EU-IMF programme at the end of 2013 and ELA is fully repaid.



19.3.5.2 Cyprus: 2011-2013

Late 2010: Cyprus Popular Bank (“Laiki”) and Bank of Cyprus (BoC) build up holdings of €5.8 billion in Greek government bonds (1/3 of Cypriot GDP).
2011: Losses wipe out Laiki’s equity and almost all of BoC’s.
October 2011: Laiki receives €2.5 billion in ELA.
February 2012: European Banking Authority communicates that Laiki needs a recapitalisation of €2 billion while BoC requires €1.5 billion.
2012: Deposits flow out, capital position worsens and ELA increases, reaching €9.6 billion in July 2012. Background negotiations on an EU-IMF programme take place but are not concluded.
In 2013,

after an election, the previous quasi-Communist government is replaced.
Post election, the ECB insists on an EU-IMF programme and bank recapitalisation as a condition for continuing ELA.
The government is judged by EU-IMF as too indebted to recapitalise banks so haircuts are applied to depositors.
Capital controls are put in place and remain there for years. ELA is strictly capped.





19.3.6 Greece: 2014-2015

2014: ECB conducts a Euro Area wide comprehensive assessment and stress test and announces the results in October 2014. It declares Greek banks solvent and have limited need for recapitalisation to meet their requirements.
2015: political uncertainty surrounding an upcoming election leads to deposit outflows from Greek banking system and ELA increases. Various Greek government-issued and government-backed assets removed from the eligible collateral list. After the election of a new left-wing government, the ECB insists that a new EU-IMF programme be put in place by new government as a condition for providing higher ELA. Greek government ends up imposing capital controls because banks do not have access to liquidity. Damage done to the economy and banking system requires further round of bank recapitalisation. Capital controls kept in place for years. ELA finally ends in 2019.



19.3.7 Questions About How ELA Has Been Practiced

Have the ECB’s procedures been clear and transparent?

Unlike regular Eurosystem operations, collateral requirements for ELA differ from case to case, depending on the NCB’s decisions and Governing Council approval.
Unclear relationship between national authorities and the ECB Governing Council.

Is ELA only provided to solvent banks?

Laiki bank was not solvent when it was provided with ELA.
Anglo solvency was dependent on Irish government support.
Should liquidity support be suspended for banks that ECB itself has declared solvent and have passed stress tests?
Why did ECB keep ELA limits in place even after banks (such as those in Cyprus and Greece) had been recapitalised?

Are decisions to limit ELA really made “on monetary policy grounds” or are some other set of criteria used?

Links between willingness to approve ELA and wider political events (Irish and Greek EU-IMF programme negotiations, Cyprus election)
